story.text:
It was a cold and snowy night. 
In the depths of a prison, a handful of patrol soldiers huddled around a single torch, rubbing their hands as they chatted. 
"Think the prisoner locked up in there will survive the night? It's bloody freezing in there." 
"Who knows? He hasn't eaten in days, though." 
"We'll be in for it if he kicks the bucket. The Grand Wizard specifically requested that he must be kept alive." A soldier waved a hand. "Never mind, I'll go take a look."

The soldier walked towards the dungeon, torch in hand. In the darkness, the torch's light flickered as if it could extinguish at any moment. 
The steps leading down to the dungeon were particularly narrow and slippery, causing him to slip and fall several times. 
"Damn it, I hate coming to this cursed place." The soldier grew increasingly irritated as he peered towards the dungeon and realized that there was still a considerable distance down the steps before he reached his destination. 
"Forget it, I'll just come back tomorrow." The soldier was about to turn back when a violent quake unbalanced his feet, followed by a deafening explosion that startled everyone awake.

"What was that...?" The soldier collapsed to the ground, paralyzed with terror. A deafening explosion tore through the prison wall, revealing a monstrous eye glaring through the jagged crack.
A ghastly voice hissed in his ear, "Who dares summon me?"
"N-not me! It wasn't me!" The soldier stammered, his hands flailing in frantic denial.
From the dungeon's abyssal depths boomed a reply: "I, Paixton, am your master."
In his final moments, the soldier glimpsed a blazing stallion bursting into the chamber. Chains shattered as Paixton mounted the creature — then vanished into the snow-laden night, leaving only embers in their wake.

story.text:
Feenja first laid her eyes on the golden-haired Theodemer at 16, across the long table of the court hall. She would never forget the prince's smiling face looking back at her.
On her 17th birthday, Theodemer gifted her his mother's necklace, promising to make her his queen one day.
At 18, they pledged their love under the withered old oak tree in the royal garden. It was the happiest day of Feenja's life.

At 20, Feenja was finally about to see Theodemer's promise come true.
Theodemer would, as the advisor had arranged, take her as his wife amid the blessings of their kinfolk, which would seal them as husband and wife recognized by the gods, never to be parted.
Following this, Theodemer would ascend to the throne amid the acclaim of all the nobility, the advisor added, with the matriarch of Penultima herself crowning him. Thus, he would become the new king of Owlestreia, with her by his side as queen.
But that moment never came.
On the morning she donned her bridal gown, an envoy of the advisor burst into her room, throwing both her and Theodemer into a death cell.

Emerging from the abyss of death before Theodemer, Feenja beheld the full spectacle of their macabre union.
Before her, a pair swathed in funeral linens was postured into a semblance of devotion by attendants neither living nor dead. The ceremony hall teemed with guests, their hushed murmurs weaving through the air, dissecting the uncanny forms of the bridal pair.
The massacre commenced with the first knell of the bell.
Distinguished ladies and gentlemen, the aged and the youthful, masters and their servants — all became quarry for the Penultima. Through the ensuing symphony of blood and shrieks, the corpselike celebrant proceeded, exchanging rings on behalf of the newlyweds.
Yet amidst the horror, the singular aspiration of her heart stood consummated. Within her freshly silenced, addled consciousness, a solitary notion took form:
At last, she and Theodemer were truly wed.

story.text:
Whisk tightens the mask on her face. 
She has just ended a battle... though calling it a battle isn't quite right, for she is not really a warrior. She is an assassin, and assassins have their own way of doing things — the quieter and quicker, the better. One swift strike for one silent kill. Dramatic battles are totally unnecessary. 
Whisk has done a great job, as usual.

Whisk is the only albino rat in the deep realms — a distinction that sets her apart from the folks and, worse still, carries heavy burdens.
Born with toxins coursing through her veins, she gained resistance to poisons, yet forever wore the mark of an outsider — unwanted and cast aside.
Only after enduring long seasons of rootless drifting was she given sanctuary by the Prophet Zeffi and pledged service to Boss Rook, finding at last a place she could call home.

Whisk often imagines what her future would look like if she could leave the Hypogean District. She'd long have left Teneebria if not for the friends she'd hang out with now and then.
Although she calls this place home, her wanderlust soul has always ached to leave this dim world for a faraway place.
Since she, unlike the rest of her kinsfolk, had no particular affection for the tribe, she immediately accepted the deal offered by Zeffi.
She shall complete a necessary quest and then travel to the world of light, to true freedom.

story.text:
Aspalta moved through the manor's veins, its secrets now laid bare to her practiced senses.
Traps were bypassed, wards sidestepped — her movements fluid as shadow itself as she pressed onward toward her target in the inner corridors.
Silence enveloped her like a cloak. This was the way of the blade, the creed of the unseen hand.
To the highborn of the Unyielding Silk, common folk were chattel. Their own lives, however, they guarded jealously — and predictably. For all their variation in power and expense, their defenses followed the same tired logic.

Conflict defined the deep elves of Teneebria — from the loftiest noble to the lowliest gutter-born soul.
And being born at the bottom meant facing the gentry with next to no recourse.
With her own eyes, Aspalta witnessed her kin fall to the blades of the Thallasen Clan. Of all her line, she alone drew breath.
And the bitter irony lingered: grown to adulthood, having pieced together whispers and secrets with dogged persistence, she still could not trace the author of that night's slaughter.

Assassinating nobles was her job, and also her hobby.
Sharp-eyed and fleet of foot, Aspalta had dealt with many targets of her loathing, and still she hadn't been caught. In this profession, being unknown was perhaps the greatest prestige of all.
She maintained ties with the rebellion, and while no deep elf could voice certainty of success, Aspalta yearned for the day she would see it: The day the Thallasen Clan's rule was toppled.

story.text:
While dawn mist still clung to the treetops of the Swaddling Forest, the goblins were already crouched on the sandstone, sharpening their scimitars — all weapons plundered from Arbortean human caravans.
Chorak, the goblin bandit leader, rode his hound around his territory. He wore a magnificent cloak and an ostentatious crown — such gaudy and expensive attire was his favorite trophies.

"Boss! Three carts coming from the east!" a goblin scout reported.
Chorak grinned, revealing a set of jagged teeth. Whenever he made that face, it meant some human caravan was in for a world of hurt.
At the piercing sound of a bone whistle, the goblin bandits surged from the mountain pass, a green tide crashing toward the caravan. The human guards' crossbow bolts pierced the throats of two goblins, but more had already leaped onto the cart roofs.
Chorak's hound snapped a guard's neck. Chorak shrieked, "Anything that enters our turf is ours!"

Under cover of darkness, Chorak was busy cataloguing his newest prizes when his scout came rushing in. "Boss! The Duchess of Arbortea has placed a bounty on your head!"
Chorak burst into roaring laughter, as though hearing a jester's finest tale. He then curled a beckoning finger. "Get a message to that Duchess: if she values her safety, she'll instruct her caravans to surrender their cargo willingly. Do that, and I might just let the guards live… Fail, and I will drown Arbortea in chaos!"

story.text:
Ozul sits silently in his chair.
His face is obscured by shadow, shrouding most of his features. A meeting is in progress. The brother of the Head of the Ptolemy family hasn't uttered a word the entire time, yet his aura of gloom is impossible to ignore.
Suddenly, his lips twitch, he whispers something to his right.
There is no one there, of course. The Ptolemy wizards are long accustomed to this.

Beyond providing occasional assistance to the Ptolemy house during emergencies, Ozul rarely engages in actions driven by personal volition. Most days, he simply sits in silent meditation within his quarters, or slips away to carry out assassinations ordered by his elder sibling.
Their parents met their end at the hands of none other than this reclusive sorcerer himself. In early childhood, Ozul endured brutal experiments at their hands, yet the outcome defied all expectations.
The boy who clawed his way back from mortality's edge ended the lives of his own progenitors. Since that day, Ozul’s capacity for concern begins and ends with his brother.

A demon walks in Ozul's shadow — a consequence of an indescribable experiment.
Its sickly-sweet aura of decay lured the son of a demon lord into the Scarlet Vale, where he was stripped of his physical form.
Facing mutual annihilation, the dying Ozul and the disembodied fiend sealed a dark pact, creating a fragile alliance built on necessity.
Trust has no place between them. Yet until death comes, their contract stands firm.

story.text:
Theodemer, as usual, passes by the tomb he shares with his wife, only to notice it is now covered in thick moss.
That is when he realizes that he has been dead for a long time.
So long that the dynasty he once sought to rule has become nothing but a bard's song, and those who had wronged him are nowhere to be found.
Hearing Feenja's soft singing nearby, Theodemer suddenly questions his purpose in this place.

The last prince of the Owlestreia Dynasty once basked in glory.
He remembered being dressed in splendid robes by servants and listening to advisors talk about his upcoming coronation and grand wedding. Despite talks of the dynasty's impending doom, the ambitious young prince believed he could change everything.
That belief shattered the morning he woke to Feenja's cries and found himself chained in the death cell of the dynasty.

Theodemer never forgot his death.
The torture, the pain, the screams, the tears, the blood, and the creepy faces of the Penultima cultists — he remembered them all too well.
The last thing he saw before his death was his fiancée's eyes wide with terror and despair.
When he awoke, Feenja was caressing his face with translucent hands, wearing the matching ring that symbolized their union in death. An aura of death surrounded them — a reminder that they were no longer among the living.
Their demise was accompanied by the fall of the Owlestreia Dynasty, a kingdom filled with sins and cries of despair.

story.text:
Sacredeia could smell the stench of hatred. 
Hatred permeated all corners of Teneebria, flourishing alongside despair and anger, and Sacredeia knew that many deep elves hated the Thallasen Clan.
As Sacredeia could smell hatred, she could always put out the first signs of conflict before they escalated into rebellion, to restore her control over the Unyielding Silk.

Her aspiration for power is only natural and reasonable, or at least that is what Sacredeia has always believed. 
Her ancestor, Norixius Thallasen, ascended to royalty through a victorious assassination. That assassination allowed the Thallasen Clan to build a new castle on the ruins of the old one, sweeping the names of those defeated into ashes. 
Having inherited this ambitious bloodline, Sacredeia naturally has a love for the crown.

To cement the deep elves' dominion below, Sacredeia would spare no cost. Having perceived a threat stirring in the deepest dark, the ruling Queen resolved to descend and quell it with her own hand.
It vexed her that this resurgence went unnoticed for so long — that the old royalty, once adversaries of the Thallasen Clan, had clawed their way back from the sepulcher.
No matter. She would simply drive them back into the silence from whence they came.

story.text:
Trolgar let out a heavy sigh. 
Another troll had fallen victim to Anima Damnum and gotten lost, and none of the other trolls knew where he had gone. Perhaps no one would ever see him again. In recent years, such situations have become more and more frequent, and the number of trolls in the tribe have been on the decline. 
As the chief, Trolgar undoubtedly feels a heavy burden on his shoulders, knowing that his tribespeople are facing extinction, but him being powerless to prevent it.

Trolgar knew from the beginning that the deal was a dangerous one. 
Scharlach, an Unstill, had approached him and offered a deal. After weighing the risks and benefits, the Mog-Nach troll chief had agreed — helping to collect the materials to revive the dragon was dangerous, but not impossible. 
Trolgar once believed that this could be the beginning of his tribe's growth, but little did he know that it would instead mark the pinnacle of their decline.

He was too young in those days. Young, burning to prove his worth and see his tribe prosper — desires that clouded the very wisdom he ought to have possessed.
Trolgor believed he could skirt any trap laid before him — if indeed any existed. With cleverness enough, he told himself, they would be but stumbling blocks to step across, never true obstacles to bar his path.
For that hubris, he has paid dearly. In mending one rent in the fabric of his people, he opened others far wider. Now, standing alone against the tide, he knows his strength is not enough. Perhaps the hour has come to humble himself before that old companion — for the sake of the clan, no pride is too great to lay down.

story.text:
Quaesitia surveyed the assembly of nobles arrayed before her.
These long years of discipline had, at last, rendered the deep elves somewhat more tolerable to her eye.
Gone, at least, were their vain attempts to obscure reality beneath layers of ornate prose in their reports — a useless endeavor from the start.
Unlike her elder sister, Sacredeia, Quaesitia harbored no patience for empty courtesies. What proved unfit, she would cull without hesitation.

Being the second daughter of Thallasen Clan, she had never originally coveted the seat.
One must weigh matters holistically: Sacredeia had done little to disgrace their lineage, while Quaesitia found distinct satisfaction in her martial duties as a general.
Nevertheless, with her elder sister gone, the mantle fell to her by necessity.
What alternative remained? Surrender the throne to Auster, that spineless incompetent? Preposterous.

Power is the purest thing, and authority is its vassal. Authority without power will only meet the most tragic of ends.
Quaesitia trusted only in her own discretion, for she was the bearer of power in the Unyielding Silk now.
She would occasionally heed Lethander's advice, but such instances were a rarity, and her advisor was hardly unintelligent.
She was quite satisfied with the status quo — if only it weren't for those lowlife rabble standing in her way.

story.text:
"Stay clear of those coastal rocks!" the old fisher intones gravely to the younger generation. Yet youth's curiosity burns with the force of a mountain wildfire.
And so he meets Aemonleyda.
There she rests upon the stone, her fin submerged beneath the waves — more radiant than any jewel adorning her form.
To the handsome young fisherman, this becomes a haunting dream he will carry all his days. To Aemonleyda, it is merely another fleeting diversion.

A hedonist at heart, Aemonleyda loves exquisite jewelry, fine wines, and passionate romances.
To indulge her tastes, she becomes a merchant, trading the treasures of the sea and the loot from sunken ships for the luxuries she desires from other races.
Dealing with land-based merchants never troubles Aemonleyda much. They are always too mesmerized by her smile and beauty, foolishly offering too much in exchange.
Watching their confusion and regret is Aemonleyda's favorite pastime apart from the transactions.

Aemonleyda parts ways with her latest romantic conquest with a smile, fully aware that this poor soul will soon be forgotten, along with his name.
To her, love is no different from fine wine — a mere indulgence to elevate her spirits.
She has an important transaction on the horizon today: a shipment of seawater-resistant weapons from the dwarven lands, brought by the Crimson Crow. These weapons are as valuable as gold itself.
But still, in Aemonleyda's eyes, she herself is always the most powerful weapon.

story.text:
Aladiah prowled across the frozen plain, pressing ahead just as the voice told her to.
Not a single other dwarf accompanied her, the only guard far from sight. This is what she needs, even though as Matriarch, she merits more protection than she has.
But as she listened to the calls of the ore veins, she needed no interruption. This is Aladiah's unique connection to this tundra. As a druid, one is bound to nature.

She is kind and magnanimous, much like her husband, Elder Huberg, and yet entirely unlike the current young clan head, Huldork.
Aladiah truly cares for her people and tangibly contributes to making their existence better.
Her prowess in finding shelter from Iskalland's howling winds, combined with her competence in stewarding her people, has firmly cemented Aladiah's position. She is the warmth of spring in the frigid winter.

In her quieter hours, Aladiah finds joy in speaking with the young ones.
Her heart holds a place for every child of the clan — even her rather stern nephew, Huldork. But none seek out her company so readily as her own daughter, Beldelle.
It pleases Aladiah to know that others among their kin call her daughter the 'Ice Sun,' for she cherishes the name herself. And when Beldelle comes near, Aladiah smiles and draws close, listening with a mother's boundless interest to whatever words might follow.

story.text:
Synarell's first memory as a young sheen elf was the Misty Sea ablaze with flames on the Day of Skyfire.
Growing up in the war-scarred Increscenta, he later joined many young elves in the Royal Guard's warrior training, where he discovered his innate talent for controlling fire.
On his 100th birthday, during his coming-of-age ceremony, he was officially inducted into the Royal Guard. Lord Thelendor himself presented him with a longsword that could conjure flames. Amid the congratulations, the sight of his homeland, the island where he was born and raised, brought back memories of the fiery sea.
That was when he realized he might be longing for something.

When the Royal Guard was selecting a cruising officer to station at Lacunae, Synarell didn't hesitate to volunteer.
His request was granted by Tharivol, the Silver Moon Sentinel, an elven ranger revered across Increscenta for his loyalty and strength. However, Synarell admired him for another reason: Tharivol was a legendary adventurer who had traveled across Adenthia. For some reason, Synarell saw himself in Tharivol's keen eyes.
Tharivol's approval led to Synarell's first voyage at sea, his first departure from Increscent, and his first time witnessing schools of fish swimming in the reflection of the sunrise.
For the first time in his life, the elf Synarell felt truly free.

Befriending a wood elf was never part of Synarell's plan, but Yfeir, the prince of Driftwood and an outlier born at sea, crashed into his life in an unreasonable manner following an embarrassing ship collision.
Yfeir showed him a world of possibilities, with adventure and many wonders beyond the Misty Sea always on his lips.
Synarell realized how similar they were — they were both standing at the intersection of inescapable duty and wild fantasies. However, no one knew what all this would lead to.
Sometimes, they would have the same dream: they saw the Misty Sea's mythals vanish under a brilliant sunrise, and the world — parts they had never seen — unfold before their eyes.

story.text:
Daphne’s world measured but a few cramped inches — a tiny jewel-casket that held the contorted spirit of a queen.
Within its confines she knew only oppression, anguish, despair… and hate.
More than once, when some hapless soul chanced upon the coffer, awareness fled her entirely, leaving only blind slaughter as the vessel of her rage and grief.
Then clarity returned, and with it the suffering grew only keener, heavier — dragging her ever downward into darkness.

Daphne once tasted glory. 
Her family hailed from the south, and from the wasteland where they founded a new dynasty. To eradicate the cultists who brought about war, the members of the Owlestreia family poured all their efforts into wiping them out. 
However, they had underestimated the enemy, which ultimately led to the destruction of their short-lived dynasty. Daphne witnessed its demise, and suffered brutal torture.

Everything began from the civil war, instigated by the cultists who manipulated the members of the royal family to kill one another. 
Daphne witnessed the fall of the dynasty, trapped in her tower. She couldn't escape. No, she should have known that to the cultists, death was not a punishment, but a new beginning. 
Daphne's body was stuffed into a small jewelry box, and her soul, tormented by pain, was under the command of her enemies. She lost her sanity... but perhaps it was a good thing.

story.text:
The tide is rising — Lincos tilts his head slightly, listening carefully to the sound of waves crashing against the rocks.
He composes a new song, drawing inspiration from the entire Misty Sea — tidal movements, ocean currents, storms, and whirlpools form a harmonious chord.
Only merfolk can sing such melodies, and only they can understand them.
It truly is a pity.

Like most of his kind, Lincos possesses a gift for song — but unlike them, he is a musician to his very soul. Performance and composition have long formed the twin pillars of his existence.
Yet in time, the known melodies ceased to suffice. He yearned for something wholly original, a flawless composition that belonged to him alone. Such creative fixation left his nerves perpetually taut, driving a wedge between himself and those he once held dear.
That changed with the ruin of Equinoxial. Its fall struck him like a plunge into the frigid currents of the northern sea — a shock that jolted him awake to stark reality.
He knows, with a certainty that runs bone-deep, that he shall someday bring forth this new song. But not yet. Not now.

The weather is splendid today. Lincos surfaces and sits on his favorite reef, singing his new song.
Carried by the sea breeze, his voice reaches a nearby cargo ship, prompting the previously lethargic sailors to quickly steer away from the area.
Lincos is saddened by his audience's retreat, unaware that among foreign sailors, there are legends of the merfolk's singing heralding the coming of storms.
In truth, he simply loves to sing in the calm before the storm.

story.text:
Nestled deep within the wilderness, far removed from the trappings of civilization, dwells a secretive tribe of ridge halflings. They inhabit the loneliest reaches, keeping company with wind and stone, closer in spirit to the mountain goats leaping among the crags than to reasoning beings.
Strangers who trouble the mountain's tranquility find no welcome here. Should one overstep under the hidden gaze of the sentinels, the warning drums would echo through the valleys, and from the unwatched shadows would emerge a cloaked figure draped in pelts, twin sickles gleaming in hand — the harvester appointed to guard this sacred solitude.
Stanguem never hesitated to kill for the safety of the tribe.

Drums are used to warn fellow tribespeople, and the double-sickle is used to remove threats. This is the duty of the vigilante, and something Stanguem firmly believes in for the survival of the tribe. Her patience and gentleness are reserved for her kin and the mountains; to her, the harsh footsteps of outsiders only break the harmony of nature, and therefore must be banished.
These greedy outlanders could only bring disaster. Such is her conviction, and she confirms it over and over again with her warning drums and blood-stained double-sickle.

Stanguem's hostility to outlanders is not without cause.
She had a little sister, but the once cherished name would never be spoken again. They used to depend on each other until an outlander tricked her sister and took her away from Stanguem's protection. In search of her sister's whereabouts, Stanguem traveled out of the mountains for the first time. Eventually, she returned alone, becoming taciturn, brooding, and irritable, and she's now the most reliable vigilante in the tribe.
The ridge halflings have had enough of outlanders. The tribe needs no change, and living with nature is the only and lasting way to survive.

story.text:
Rook tapped the smoking pipe in his claw, blowing out a faint puff of white smoke. 
The giant rat serving as a seat for the Boss of the Three Ears seemed to sense his master's emotions, and let out a threatening snarl. Rook whistled at it, and it immediately quietened down. 
"Well then," Rook said with a smirk, "Tell me, my guest, what are your terms for this deal?"

His beginnings were shaped by his adoptive mother, the prophet Zeffi. Her selfless nurturing of orphans united the ratfolk of the Hypogean District, and Rook, as her ward, swiftly gathered a following of his own.
Yet the climb to his present station demanded far more — much more.
That kindly smile never leaves his face, not even when his words deliver death.

Rook demands absolute dominion over all he claims as his own — a category that includes his ward, Twitch.
Though he himself slew the boy’s parents, such acts are commonplace in the Hypogean District; among the elven houses of the Unyielding Silk, they are scarcely worth noting.
He needed only a pretext, a plausible justification, to mend the fissure his deed had created — and fortune provided one, sufficiently credible to serve.
As the master of the Three Ears, Rook savors the pleasures of existence. Yet to preserve this life of privilege, he wields political machination and orchestrated murder not as evils, but as mere instruments of his will.

story.text:
Upon the Celestial Isle, at the apex gazed upon by all, a solitary tower has endured for millennia. Adventurers beyond count have sought its secrets in vain.
Even after braving laser turrets and treacherous puzzle-labyrinths, the last and deadliest challenge awaits: a ballet performance.
Any soul hearing this account voices the same bewilderment: "How could ballet be perilous… No, rather, how does a ballet come to be staged here?"
To this day, those survivors remember that moment — their hearts hammering like war drums, beholding a spectacle both terrifying and irresistibly enthralling.

"Guest presence confirmed. Banquet sequence initiated."
With those words, the great curtains parted. A procession of construct attendants streamed forth, trailed by the majordomo. Last to enter were the dancers, arrayed in breathtaking finery.
With the company assembled, the moment arrived for the prima ballerina's entrance.
To a cascade of crystalline notes, she ascended the stage, rotating in flawless arcs with an ethereal grace. An intense, dreamlike radiance emanated from her — a sapphirine glow so dazzling it pained the eyes.
At last, attaining the exact center, she dipped into a deep curtsy. "My honored guests, I am Guinavivre. I dedicate this final performance to you."

Everything that followed happened so suddenly that no matter how hard the adventurers tried to remember, they couldn't recall how the tragedy began.
The music played on, the dance never ceased, and the construct banquet seemed to continue, but the intruding adventurers fell one by one.
Blood traced a graceful arc through the air, splattering silently. It wasn't until the metallic tang hit their nostrils that the adventurers realized danger was upon them.
Without touching the floor, she twirled silently and swiftly in her perfect form. Wherever she passed, their companions fell with entranced smiles.
At the end of the tale, the lucky one furthest from the stage finally acted — though by his own account, it was an instinctual reaction faster than thought. He mustered the greatest speed of his life and chanted a teleportation spell.
The memory finally concludes. The adventurer summarizes his tale — to this day, the most vivid impression in his mind is not the bodies of his companions, but that brilliant, sapphire-like light.

story.text:
"Boss... must we truly cross this tempest just to peddle our wares?"
"The fiercer the gale, the greater the gain." Victor met their trepidation with the old adage he so often wielded.
He was a man unafraid of the ocean's wrath. It was precisely his keen mercantile instinct and a daring spirit outstripping every rival that had carved his reputation into these shores — though whether it was a reputable one was quite another matter.

He understands risk intimately — even embraces it — yet draws a stark line at outright loss.
Consider the automaton Mekkatorque: a venture doomed from conception to completion.
Research and trade ought to serve one another, yet when knowledge outstrips coin, sparks inevitably fly.
As a merchant, he demands one clear return from the labs he funds: gold. Solid, predictable, and unfailingly faithful.

His daughter used to question his beliefs.
His sweet girl was such a naive, confident, and idealistic young scientist. He still can't forget the sight of her carrying a tool kit bigger than herself and boarding the Mekkashon without looking back.
That was the last time he ever saw her.
"Captain! We made it through the thunderstorm and reached the disaster-stricken island!" A cheer goes up around them. Bathed in the worshipful gazes of his crew, Victor methodically directs the crowd to the island.
The merchant never dwells on the past; his sole concern now is selling the present goods at a substantial markup.

story.text:
For millennia untold, Diantha has delighted in shifting shape — now a sigh of wind, now a bloom, now a bee or butterfly… becoming each fleeting aspect of the woodland realm.
By daylight, she drifts amid flower-beds, overhearing blossoms bicker over a honeybee's erratic route; by dusk, she peers into a bear's den, quietly counting its store of winter provisions...
She is a child of this ancient wood, bound to it by primal essence. To guard its sanctity is her foremost charge.
"Surely," she once reasoned, "the leaf-cloaked elves of the grove share my purpose. Can we not bear this guardianship together?"
Such misplaced faith, however, would birth a calamity beyond reckoning. Now, as a vile mist thickens and loathsome creatures defile the trees, Diantha understands, with a sinking finality, the depth of her error.

"This pelt will fetch a fine sum of gold... enough to keep me in drink for a month! Ha!" The poacher gloated over his drugged quarry, oblivious to the thorn-laden vine slithering silently around his ankle.
Fury burned cold in Diantha's gaze. Just as the curved blade descended toward the helpless beast, she gave a slight gesture. The man was jerked upside down into the air.
Swiftly, the tendrils cocooned him completely. Blood seeped between the twists, falling to the earth where the soil drank it deeply.
"May you feed this wood in agony — a tribute justly earned." The chrysalis convulsed, its struggles ignored as she roused the bear with a whispered rune and faded back into the trees.

Once more, a child strayed into her woods. Humans were always so fragile, so obstinate — yet still she drifted after him, a silent guardian behind the leaves.
When the undergrowth stirred, the boy turned to flee, only to halt after a few paces. He spun back, jaw tight, and muttered to the shadows: "I am no craven..."
His defiance died half-spoken. A grey wolf lunged, seizing his tunic in its jaws, bearing him to the earth. Fangs gleamed, poised to tear at the soft flesh of his throat.
Diantha alighted beside the creature, laying a calming hand upon its head. To the ashen-faced boy, she said softly, "Your adventure ends here. Go home now... and remember this as but a dream."
Darkness claimed him swiftly. When his eyes fluttered open once more, he was safe in his own bed, the memory of the wildwood fading like morning mist.

story.text:
Ardreth has judged many of her kin.
When awake, she hardly ever lowers the spear in her grip. Daring outlanders and elves who defy the Crescent's will shall find themselves summarily impaled.
The elves of the Aethercairn worship the moonlight, of which she is the guardian.
But considering the drawn-out years, this Arbiter isn't inclined to resort to force. Rules should be observed by all, yet, ensuring their efficacy requires a more judicious approach.

She belongs to the Crescent Order, and more often than not, she is solely at Mithrasea's side.
Even this far removed from the turmoil,  Increscent still bears the turbulent undertow.
The Silvery Tower Ardreth is in and Thelendor's Increscenta co-exist in a fragile power balance.
Thus, for the sake of keeping the balance, Ardreth is not free to act as she pleases. Consequently, this has meant the Arbiter has to turn a blind eye to certain happenings.

Ardreth feels unable to truly judge the world's sins, given that she has already allowed corruption to creep in for the sake of compromise.
Since her morality cannot be faultless, as the Arbiter, she simply maintains the stance of doing only what is necessary.
She dislikes outlanders, even the once-related wood elves, born of the same lineage as the island elves eons ago.
The Crescent doesn't protect everyone, but since Mithrasea has tacitly agreed to provide aid, Ardreth does not intend to fail her priestess.

story.text:
Durem gestured to his crew, and "Free Hatred" quickly turned, tracing a graceful arc between the clouds. 
The aerial dwarves once again returned with full loads, with box after box of Nuclear Gold loaded onto the ship. 
"We can kick back tonight, lads," said Durem as he straightened his wind-blown beard, "But don't revel too hard — there's work tomorrow!"

Everyone calls Durem "Stoutbeard", and he holds a great influence on the entire aerial dwarf clan. 
His fleet's exceptional mobility had torn through the once chaotic skies, eventually uniting the previously divided aerial dwarves. Later, they established the "Sky Code", the sole lawbook of the skies, which became the foundation of the aerial dwarves' rise. 
From then on, Durem has been publicly hailed as their leader.

Durem always dresses impeccably, in stark contrast to his rough and tumble crew. 
However, he isn't as much of a stickler for rules as his appearance suggests. In fact, Durem's verdicts may not always be in accordance with the Sky Code, but they are always made in the best interests of the greater good. 
Durem looks down upon the inflexible and conservative dwarves on the ground. He likes the sky, where everything is vaster, and freer.

story.text:
Deep within the Ellinkhern Valley — known to outsiders as the Scarlet Vale — lies a place whose very name chills the blood. Hidden in the sunless bowels of the vale, shielded by layers of arcane seals and dwarven-forged steel, this prison holds what the world dares not loose.
Here languish the mad scholars who delved too deep, the amoral pioneers who shattered ethics for progress, and the grotesque creations of minds unmoored from reason. All are bound within its lightless heart.
And Malak? He is the warden of this immense, imposing prison. Or perhaps, its living incarnation.

Malak had lived long indeed — by minotaur reckoning, his lifespan now stretched across four generations. This boon — for lack of a better term — sprang from an ancient covenant between his people and the humans of the Vale.
Their sanctuary came at a price: the construction of an impregnable prison to house the valley’s forbidden secrets, guarded by minotaur bloodlines through the ages. The prison’s existence was bound to each warden’s life-thread — a tether that meant, barring death by forbidden arts, a warden might endure as Malak had.

Malak was no bloodthirsty executioner — he saw himself as nothing more than a keeper of order. So long as prisoners remained docile within their cells, he stood unmoving as the valley's ancient cliffs, indifferent to their very existence.
Yet transgressors could never accept eternal confinement. Those who fell to Malak's hand were none but rule-breakers who'd sealed their own fate.
In all his centuries of vigil, only one captive ever walked free from those accursed gates unharmed. That moment — when the crimson-haired mage strode past the prison's grim portcullis, still wearing the same arrogant sneer as the day he entered, returning to his retinue's embrace without so much as a backward glance — would haunt Malak's memory until the end of days.

story.text:
"This Lotus of Jade was a gift from the Celestial Court and has been my ritual implement for a hundred years. Now, I shall refine it with the Samadhi Fire and give it a name — Naro."
"From now on, Naro shall be my one and only direct disciple. All other members of Mount Cangxuan, regardless of seniority, shall be his juniors."
In the year of his birth, Naro rode upon the Empyrean Treads, draped in the Blazeforged Sash. He rescued the weak, vanquished evil, and brought justice to the land. The name of this spirited prodigy was known throughout the Eastern Continent.
But one day, everything fell silent. It was said that Naro killed his adoptive father — General Zheng, who had embezzled military funds.
Overcome with grief, Naro's adoptive mother threatened suicide to demand justice for her husband.
Naro, however, insisted that the embezzlement was a grave crime, punishable by death. To repay the kindness of being raised, Naro cut flesh from his own shoulder for his adoptive mother, severing all ties.
Watching his adoptive mother's gaunt figure retreat, memories of the past flooded his mind. The account book Master Qingwei had given him felt hot against his chest.
That was the first time he doubted. "Is any of this real? Why are the people my master speaks of so different from my memories... Could there have been a mistake?"

"The Myriad Fox died by Naro's pike... Naro's a violent one. Even Master Qingwei's five hundred disciples couldn't subdue the Myriad Fox. But Naro, single-handedly, took its life in mere moments."
"But the Myriad Fox was a good demon. Last year, when the south city flooded, it used its stone-cloud magic to hold back the torrent and save the whole city. Why... did it meet such an end?"
"I heard it was caught eating children at night by Master Qingwei. Naro was ridding the world of evil!"
"No, no, that's not right. The Myriad Fox isn't like that. Naro's gone mad and is just looking for an excuse to kill! I think there's something wicked about that boy. He killed General Zheng before, and that was his adoptive father. Naro is an ungrateful traitor!"
"Hey, keep it down. Mount Cangxuan is just outside. There might be one of Naro's fellows around."
It wasn't a fellow who snitched. Naro himself was at the next table, listening to their chatter. He wasn't angry. As the saying goes, "My deeds are my own. My name is for others to speak as they will."
He silently stood up and placed a tael of silver on the table. A cup of tea cost twenty copper coins; the rest was a tip for the apprentice.

"If one day you discover that you're not enforcing heaven's will or upholding justice... but merely clearing the path for someone else's ambition, what... would you do?"
Rhaellon's icy voice rang in his ears. She shed her majestic air, looking at her old friend with serene simplicity.
"No... that can't be." Naro sat on the reef, his voice uncertain.
No one could easily deny Naro's past and beliefs, until his master told him, "Rhaellon is using the lives of all to force the Celestial Court's hand. Go with me at once to pacify the Mirrorsea of Splendor."
Remembering Rhaellon's casual question from long ago, Naro hesitated. He disobeyed his master's command, citing the need for seclusion.
Rhaellon perished... The mighty Sea Dragon Queen was reduced to no trace at all — it was a tragic end.
Naro looked at his master's radiant face, and the seed of doubt buried deep in his heart quickly sprouted. His master was no match for Rhaellon in magical power, and the Oceanic Pearl held divine power. How could Rhaellon have died?
You are my only master, the one who enlightened me. I never wanted to doubt you, but this and everything else doesn't add up...
"Naro, the Oceanic Pearl is evidence. Find it and bring it back untouched. Do not come into contact with it too much." What are you afraid of, Master?

story.text:
Nissa suppressed her impatience as she handed the new and improved crossbow to her subordinate. 
The brilliant Blue Magic Crystal on it illuminated a small area in the darkness of the Hypogean District, though the gnomes who had lived here for a long time were already accustomed to seeing in the dark. 
Lately, Nissa's mood had been quite terrible due to the expanding trade of the ratfolk. Since they insisted on dumping those addictive goods on her tribe, Nissa was done being polite.

Most gnomes in the Hypogean District trust Nissa, a reliable and generous leader. 
One's status is determined by their value, and the Mechanical Light Crossbow she invented has become the most popular weapon among the gnomes due to its convenience. 
Although Nissa can be rash in her actions, she is still meticulous. In Teneebria, survival is no easy feat for any tribe, and having an excellent leader is of utmost importance.

Nissa had stood witness to the gnomes' darkest hour in the Hypogean District.
When the deep elves' first assault nearly shattered their people, it was Nissa who shouldered leadership's weight — and still bears it today. Her inventions favor brutal utility over cleverness, survival over sophistication.
Years of toil have etched their price upon her: failing vision she stubbornly conceals, as if denying weakness might undo its creeping advance.

During this time, all enemies hit by a Lightning Chain within the field take damage twice, with the second instance of damage reduced by 50%.

story.text:
The rusty stench of the iron cage swallowed her first cries.
After branding her shoulder blade with a number, the orcs outside the cage took away her mother, who had just given birth. Clueless, she sucked on bloody straw, spending her first night — or countless nights — in this world.
A half-human, half-orc body was too frail. She couldn't tear apart prey like orc cubs, nor could she fetch a good price like pure-blooded humans.
Her mother always fed her the thin gruel, gnawing on moss from the wall cracks herself — until one snowy night, those withered hands could no longer lift the dirty bowl.

She could not say when it began — those whispers of the dead that now haunted her days. Perhaps her hollow existence had blurred the line between the living and the departed.
The first clear visitation came at ten winters old. Warhorses shrieked alongside spectral wails, jolting her awake: "The imperial host approaches — flee!" Straw prickled her skin as she burrowed deep, the orcs' slaughter of prisoners echoing through the hut.
Time lost meaning until human hands dragged her from the corpse-mound. The officer's pity reeked of hypocrisy — she knew its price: another collar, another master.
So she drove her hidden blade into the gilded knight's eye and fled her captors — joining the ranks of the restless dead.

The Bearheart Lamp continuously pumps out ghostly blue flames — the still-beating heart of the Bear King.
If anyone gets close to the lamp, they'd find a crack on its surface, a mark left by her dagger years ago.
Wandering the wilderness alone, she stumbled into the Bear King's cave and defeated it in a life-for-life battle. She thought her life would end there, but the whispers of the departed souls sounded again — clearer than ever before. No longer a cacophony, but a single voice, distant yet near.
It invited her to make a deal, and she accepted.
To this day, no one has discovered this secret. Those fools who tried to approach her with gold or love ended up as minced meat between the bears' teeth — after all, long before she learned to speak, Bernade had mastered the law of the jungle.

During the charge, if any target on the field dies, Natural Instinct will be granted to all summoned units and Summoner School heroes.

story.text:
Beldelle ducked behind her father, cheeks burning. A few minutes later, and her best friend might’ve been frozen solid.
"Just roughhousing — no harm done! See? Still in one piece," Gerthin said, waving it off.
But the angry red patches on Gerthin’s skin told another story. Beldelle’s stomach twisted.
Why couldn’t she get this right? Why did her magic always spiral out of control? How long before everyone got sick of her blunders?

For three long months, Beldelle locked herself away, deaf to all pleas to come out.
Her mother, Aladiah, fretted helplessly — left with no choice but to set meals by the door, knock softly, and walk away.
The endless clatter and explosions from within told Huberg all he needed to know: his coddled daughter was forging her own path now. Grown, and determined to face her trials alone.
When Beldelle finally emerged, her armor gleamed with pristine frost. With a triumphant spin, she announced: "I’ve tamed the ice at last!"

"Cheers! On a day this special, no hiding behind milk!" Gerthin raised her tankard, laughter bubbling through the room.
Beldelle sighed. Gods, I must be the worst drinking dwarf alive.
The liquor burned its way down. Two small cups in, her thoughts grew fuzzy — but her heart soared. Soon she was belting out songs, hugging everyone in sight, dragging them into retellings of her father’s tales... until the world faded to black.
She woke in her own bed, memories rushing back. A grin spread across her face. No more holding back — she can hug them all she want now.

story.text:
The pages whispered through Perkunte’s fingers, their faint rustling stirring a breeze that never reached his armored skin.
His time among the tomes had ended, and he made to retreat to his chambers high in the Great Library’s vaulted halls.
Yet his departure met interruption — a wizard from beyond the Scarlet Vale, who halted him with questions. To answer was no trial, for they touched upon a past he had walked himself.

The wizard clans in the Scarlet Vale are quite familiar with Perkunte, and they'd warmly embrace his arrival. 
After all, this young wizard always offers intriguing insights and communicates in a mild and respectful manner, even earning the respect of the more peculiar wizards. 
However, this isn't only because of the knowledge he offers, but also because of the powerful energy this secluded wizard exudes.

Perkunte had once accounted for his origins — that peculiar aura clinging to him. Yes, he claimed distant lands, draconic blood drunken in ceremony, power wrested from ancient rites.
All lies. Every syllable.
When he'd tumbled into the Material Plane, he'd been scarcely more than a whelp. Memories of the Upper Realms had blurred like ink in rain. Yet never had he forgotten his purpose — the very reason he sought the Vale: To find his way home.

story.text:
The golden curse brand sank inwards, evoking a resentful grunt from Aschetius. He clenched his fists tightly, the long shackles binding his arms rattling and clanking.
The lava flowing around his perch bubbling up furiously with his change of mood, as if seething along with him, melting the rocks.
Most of the time, Aschetius sits and seethes, his temperament unpredictable. Even his devotees are daunted by it.

Once a loyal vassal to the Dragon Queen, Aschetius now endures his volcanic exile — an eternity measured in molten centuries.
The lizardfolk worship his dominion over flame and magma — yet their adoration rings hollow. His ambition burns singular: to reclaim his stolen divinity and escape this suffocating mortal realm.
That these feeble creatures mistake him for a sun god — the irony would amuse, were he not so consumed by purpose.

In elder days, Aschetius bore little resemblance to the wrathful being he now embodies.
His descent into this capricious malice stems from one singular torment — the theft of his power. To a soul that worshipped strength, no fate cuts deeper.
Nor has he forgotten the architect of his ruin — that entity from chaos’ darkest gulfs who once laid him low.
When regained power courses through his veins — should fate decree their paths cross anew — this time, the ending shall be rewritten.

story.text:
Every year, the Academy's admission list is populated by a handful of prodigies. Most of them are full of hot air, fading into obscurity a couple of short years after making their initial splash.
Rose, however, is a prodigy among prodigies. She brings together two seemingly unrelated elements: being a halfling and possessing magic. However, after her own initial splash, she, too, seemed to be on the same path as those other declining geniuses...

Rose’s brilliance had not waned in the slightest. In under a year, she’d devoured the Academy’s libraries with a halfling’s appetite for feasts — yet she left before finals could test her, summoned away by a mentor’s grand task: Reclassify all thaumaturgy across Adenthia.
She set off with a scholar’s pack and a traveler’s grin, hungry for the road’s lessons.
Let her never discover, the mentor mused, that "grand task" was but a ruse to exile an exhaustingly bright mind — and reclaim his peace.

Cheerful, optimistic, kind to a fault, brimming with energy yet utterly tactless — once seized by an enthralling topic, she'd chatter without end... Rose embodied every quintessential halfling trait. It was the crucible of real-world experience that tempered her brilliance into something far more luminous.
Her small stature proved an unexpected boon, allowing her to unearth forgotten incantations and arcane sigils in crumbling ruins — all meticulously recorded in that massive grimoire she insisted on calling "The Cookbook."
Oh, how we anticipated the moment — that glorious thunk of her mentor's jaw meeting the floor when Rose finally marched back into the Academy, her trove of rediscovered magic in hand.

story.text:
Who hasn't dreamt of following a faded treasure map, finding legendary riches and living a life of ease and fortune?
Long ago, a young woman born into poverty harbored such a dream. She joined an expedition formed by the queen of an ancient desert kingdom, venturing deep into the sands to seek the royal treasure.
Gladys was undoubtedly fortunate. No sandstorms barred their path, no terrifying monsters ambushed them. The party reached the ruins hiding the treasure without incident.
It seemed too easy, almost a divine sign! Eager for a larger share, Gladys volunteered to open the chest. As seal after seal was broken, she discovered... the smooth journey was merely a beautiful trap.
An ancient curse poured into Gladys's body. She distinctly heard the queen's hollow, wicked laughter echoing in her ears: "Finally, someone to inherit this gift — immortality! Taste the flavor of eternal youth!"

How could eternal youth be a curse? The young Gladys dismissed the thought. That is, until her parents, her lover, her children... grew old and frail, eventually letting go of her still-youthful hand.
To find some amusement in her endless life, Gladys embarked on adventures once more. Mountains, forests, ice fields... Gladys's footprints covered every corner of Adenthia.
Until at last, no scenery could stir a flicker of wonder in her. Finding everything dull and uninteresting, she returned to the desert, hoping to find a way to break the curse. But the ancient kingdom had long been buried by sandstorms.
Facing the boundless yellow sands, Gladys admitted for the first time: immortality was indeed a curse. All things have their end. But what about me?
To break the curse, she soon founded the guild, Crimson Crow, with a halfling friend in the desert. "With the wisdom of countless adventurers gathered," she reasoned, "surely I can find what I seek."

Rumor has it that Gladys is skilled in divination and knows the secrets of heavens. Countless royals and nobles offer vast sums of gold and jewels, begging her to guide their future.
For the sake of the guild, Gladys occasionally meets these dignitaries. But she always politely declines requests for divination. "Destiny does not bend to mortal will. What meaning is there in knowing or not knowing?"
One late night, a mysterious noble appeared at her door, insisting she divine the outcome of his impending coup. Seeing no way out, she obliged.
Gladys placed the compass gently before the noble. "Focus, listen to the voice within your heart. The compass will guide you to the answer."
Looking at the noble's devout eyes, Gladys chuckled inwardly: Divination? It's actually reading minds.

story.text:
Before Zhorak undertook his quest for the dragons, the clan chief had warned: "You won't return alive."
So what? If he could find a true dragon's remains, Zhorak would gladly pay with his bones.
A thousand miles he trekked alone, his clothes worn to threads, his stomach hollow with hunger — until at last he clawed his way up the ice-clad peak. Then came the roar, the avalanche's fist hurling him toward the cliff's edge.
And as he fell, a thought: What if this too is the dragon's will?
The hidden cave swallowed him whole. There, glowing in the darkness, lay the sacred skeleton.

Zhorak staggered forward, the dragon bone heavy on his shoulder. His body was a map of cuts and scrapes from the rocks, the scent of blood drawing a dozen snarling jackals into a tightening circle.
He reached for his axe — his faithful companion in countless battles — but now it might as well have been forged from lead. With a silent prayer, he shut his eyes.
Then — light. The bone at his back flared, its glow seeping into his wounds, through his veins, until his very blood hummed with it. It must be the dragon's blessing, he thought wildly.
When he opened his eyes, the jackals were already frozen mid-snarl, their hunger preserved in ice.

Zhorak had never cared for tribal squabbles, preferring to study the doctrines alone. Other orcs, mistaking his serenity for weakness, saw him as a pitiful coward — so many challenged him to duels.
To these blustering clansmen, Zhorak paid no heed; such childish displays weren't worth his attention.
Until the day an orc stormed his tent and set flame to every parchment on his desk.
"To scorn the doctrine is to scorn the Dragon Gods. All who slight them shall be judged." With that, Zhorak raised his scepter, severed the offender's head, and hung it from a pillar. The tribe erupted in fury.
When the altar pillars grew thick with orcish heads, Zhorak himself had vanished without a trace.

story.text:
Shai'nachtan let out a disgruntled noise as he surveyed the pile of remains which were once his teammates. Clearly, they were all dead. 
Teammates... were temporary, of course. This was just one of the ways Shai'nachtan amused himself, and it was one of his favorites. 
Occasionally, Shai'nachtan would walk into a random tavern, drink a few rounds, and inquire about the most enticing but troublesome commission around the area. He would then use his glib tongue to persuade a group of like-minded adventurers who pursued danger and wealth to embark on an expedition with him.

Every sovereign he'd served proved insufferably dull — kings and queens alike were but gilded fools upon their thrones.
Shai'nachtan found the lizardfolk's company intolerable beyond measure. Conformity to their tribal ways wasn't beyond his capability — merely beneath his contempt. His path followed only the wild whispers of his untamed soul.
"Oh, pitiful creatures! When life grants but one performance, why cower in the wings?"

Though death held no finality for him, ennui still gnawed at Shai'nachtan's bones.
Countless schemes simmered in his mind — untested wonders, unproven theories. And yes, death's embrace numbered among them.
He chased peril's sweet sting, reveled in his dance along oblivion's razor-edge. Did none cheer his spectacular performance? No matter! His own hands would thunder applause.

story.text:
Karf grinned and let out a whistle. 
His crew quickly sprang into action, securing the ropes and adjusting the angles of the cannons, then waited for the captain of the Banshee's signal to fire. Karf did not rush to do so, for he was a very patient man — especially so when his prey was within range, as such patience was necessary and crucial. 
Karf surveyed his crew — each face brimming with thirst and desire for wealth and freedom — and gave the signal.

Karf’s birthplace was wretched — but then again, every child raised in the gutter thinks they’ve drawn the worst lot. There’s only "bad" and "worse" down there, and pride clings to the belief you’re the latter.
Dragonsaerie’s glittering towers and gold-lined streets meant nothing to the dregs below. Misfortune, once set in motion, doesn’t bend for poetic endings — no last-minute rescues, no bards’ merciful edits.
So Karf grew sharp-tongued and sharper-witted, surviving on both. Until the day even that wasn’t enough — until the pirates came.

Karf knew plenty of thrilling tales — but stories only survive when their heroes do.
When the pirates took him, he didn’t despair. Instead, he learned the ropes fast — so fast that within months, a quick, brutal mutiny turned him from captive to captain.
He’d heard the legends, of course: the romance, the adventure, the sheer absurdity of it all. But Karf still wanted in. Better to live loud and die grinning than fade into some dull, forgettable end.

story.text:
Shinnah stands mute, watching her kin’s remains descend into Leviathan Hollow’s embrace.
Though merfolk weave songs like sea-foam, she keeps her silence at every funeral rite.
No grief is needed, since death is but flesh returning home — sinking slow into the welcoming depths.
And the soul? Oh, the soul grows luminous — rising, joyous, weightless — until it dances forever in the sun-painted currents.

Even in her youth, Shinnah would venture alone into the ocean’s untamed depths — where sunlight dared not linger.
Unlike her playmates, she believed her voice lacked their silver-toned grace, though they insisted otherwise.
Yet song held little allure for her restless spirit — why labor over scales when uncharted trenches whispered promises of discovery?
The sea’s secrets outstripped even merfolk knowledge, its abyssal mysteries still veiled. But it was precisely this thirst for the unexplored — this hunger to resurrect drowned histories — that would chart Shinnah’s singular course.

From the current's depths, she gazed across Leviathan Hollow — the place where all merfolk would eventually return to, their final resting place.
Shinnah wondered where they, the merfolk, had come from, and why they had chosen Leviathan Hollow as their final destination.
She spent her time alone reading all those scrolls, and, when she grew up, she became the mayor of this silent town.
Shinnah considers presiding over funerals to be a divine rite, and that the only way to honor death is to evoke an equivalent appreciation for life.

story.text:
When the third wave of adventurers disappeared into the swamp's hungry depths, the terrified villagers erected sturdy warning posts at every forest path's mouth. A silent dread now choked the woodland settlement, its people clinging to one hope: that the departing Crimson Crow courier might bring back mightier warriors from beyond to end their nightmare.
Yet scarcely had the courier's hoofbeats faded when foul, reeking arms erupted from the roadside's putrid leaf-muck. Dalk's shrill laughter slithered through the trees as he wiped pus-streaked flesh, tossing picked-clean human bones onto the path like discarded twigs.
Grinning wide enough to split his rotting cheeks, the creature wriggled free from his fetid nest. With jerking, insectile movements, he scuttled from the wood — hungry for fresh prey, for new corruption, for company in his eternal decay.

Dalk had long ceased to remember his ancestral home. Yet memory, cruel in its persistence, refused to erase those days entirely. Once, he had been an ordinary troll — hating outsiders, shunning the world beyond, occasionally procuring foreign flesh for ancestral rites like his frost-dwelling kin. Until the morass took him. No, not mere mire — that yawning abyss that passed for swamp.
The fall peeled his skin like rotten bark. Bones dissolved into the ooze as some primordial foulness crept into his marrow, unraveling mind and reason both, then spewed what remained back into the world — a thing no longer troll, but nightmare given form.
When he awoke sprawled in sunlight, it was as some great beast's rejected bile. His scream pierced the air, for the light that once nurtured now only scorched.

The metamorphosis demanded time — for Dalk to reconcile with his new being, or perhaps for the world to warp into alignment with his ruined perception. Emerging from the abyssal mire, he discovered a universal truth: the world's stench mirrored his own. All was putrescence; all deserved annihilation. This revelation became his crusade — to accelerate the decay he saw everywhere, even as he ravaged his own flesh with equal fervor.
Through festering bogs and lightless crevices he slithered, reducing travelers to screaming husks, dragging warriors' remains into the depths. The world was corruption. He was corruption. All living things should share this glorious fate.
What remained of beauty? His thoughts now festered like his flesh. Yet memory preserved one treasure: the discordant strains of a broken instrument, heard while crouched in sewer filth. That fleeting cacophony had pleased him — or the things writhing within him. Yes, beauty survived thus: in rotten notes from rotten things.

story.text:
The first time Sleight set foot in Dragonsaerie, he made a vow. The gleaming cathedral spires, the diverse jewels at the market, the fresh fish supplied daily at the port — one day, he would bring his brothers from the Three Ears to enjoy this bounty!
Back then, the Three Ears Brotherhood hadn't yet made its name. He and Rook had just secured the first piece of territory for the ratfolk in Teneebria. With treacherous deep elves ahead and stubborn gnomes behind, life wasn't easy for the ratfolk.
But Sleight knew that to truly make the Three Ears strong, the underground wasn't enough.

When he shouldered his heavy pack and bid Rook farewell, Rook didn't say much and just gave him a long embrace. He knew the mess Rook faced, and Rook knew why he chose to leave.
In this world where the strong prey on the weak, ratfolk seemed naturally disadvantaged. But they weren't weak; they just needed to move with more cunning.
Just as the name "Three Ears" implied — the unassuming ratfolk would always be the third ear, listening in the shadows, unnoticed by others.

Dragonsaerie, Arbortea, Anzuluvon — even the distant expanse of the Misty Sea — bore witness to Sleight's relentless passage across every league of Adenthia.
He built his dominion through the trade of secrets and purloined treasures, his words shifting like mercury to suit merchants or ratfolk alike. While the Crimson Crow maintained their honorable codes, the Three Ears acknowledged but a single creed: payment dictates principle.
Thus did the empire's whispered truths travel — from the damp shadows where ratfolk conspire to the farthest reaches of the realm — until every adventurer nursing dark designs came to revere the name of Three Ears.

story.text:
The historians of the continent are all familiar with the rise and fall of the Owlestreia Dynasty. 
In the long history of the continent, it is not uncommon for blood relatives to turn against each other in internal royal strifes, leading to tragic downfalls of numerous kingdoms. However, the story of the Unclean Dynasty still leaves a mark in historical records that cannot be ignored. 
This short-lived dynasty, which lasted only a hundred years, earned the name "Unclean" due to its horrifying demise. 
Its false king, the cause of it all, had been struck by a curse that turned him into a skeleton. To this day, he still wanders the ruins of his capital in lament and hatred, futilely attempting to resurrect his long-dead kingdom.

It was the Penultima. The Penultima was responsible for everything. 
If the Penultima had never existed, his mind would never have conjured such traitorous thoughts against his mediocre brother... 
If the Penultima had never existed, the princess who had lost her husband would never have cursed him out of heartbreak, when he put his brother's bloodstained crown upon his head... 
If the Penultima had never existed, his body would never have turned into a skeleton, and his subjects would never have perished in a torrent of curses, and his kingdom would never have turned into ruins overnight... 
If the Penultima had never existed... he could have escaped the curse of immortality and been freed from his endless resentment... 
The Penultima... The Penultima... You shall pay the price in blood!

A lone monarch roams endlessly through the ruins of his fallen kingdom, burdened by his heinous sins, muttering curses, and yearning for an impossible revenge. His obsession finally receives a response — from a mighty black dragon who descends upon the ruins. 
The black dragon offers Irzillas a new promise: the destruction of the Penultima, as well as an everlasting kingdom. 
The lamenting monarch is relegated to being a guard of the ruins, though he firmly believes that this subservience is only temporary. The black dragon will keep his promise. Everything that he rightfully deserved in the distant past will finally be in his grasp, after all this time.

story.text:
A guttural wail erupted from Rhash's throat.
In this lifeless wasteland, the searing heat tormented him, penetrating flesh to scorch the very bones beneath.
He could feel the fire raging inside him—every moment threatening to char his organs to cinders, yet they never quite did. That torment was worse than outright destruction.
The orc wanderer dared not reveal weakness before other creatures, knowing it would invite attack. Here, alone, his anguish finally found voice.

He devoured the beast's flesh.
The battle had been brutal. Following orcish tradition, Rhash celebrated his victory — feasting on its meat, then carving its bones into a longbow.
Yet the orc never knew: the beast's maniacal fury stemmed from a fire sprite's curse burning through its veins.
Now that same infernal scourge coursed through his own blood.

An old veteran, Rhash was expelled from his tribe and has roamed the plains ever since.
No other tribe would tolerate him, and he wouldn't reduce himself to their level. Compassion? That's the most worthless thing of all.
Yet, despite years of suffering the excruciating pain of searing flesh, the orc never relented.
Rhash continued his journey to lift the curse, with no intent on stopping for anything less than death.

story.text:
Under the sparkling fireworks at the square, the young nobleman finally summons the courage to approach the girl sitting in the corner, Vinyara. He edges closer with shuffling steps, pondering nervously about what the best to talk about with this attractive young woman. Then, a firework bursts into the Dragonsaerie night sky.
In that flash, the young man no longer sees a beautiful lady sitting there, but a ghastly sight with jutting cheekbones and hollow eye sockets. He blinks. Everything is back to normal. The young nobleman falters, hesitating for a moment, before trotting back into the crowd, trembling.

She is known by names too numerous to count.
Having followed her master from the chaotic abyss, Vinyara has served many roles throughout Adenthia's vast history. She has entered the subterranean citadels, and trodden frost-covered earth.
History is like the surface of calm waters, rippled and stirred by Vinyara, and plunged into turbulent currents of bubbling swells.
So much fun! Vinyara is fond of the responsibilities entrusted to her. She could be anything in existence, she could be nothing at all. So much fun.

Even before kissing the chaos, Vinyara had been a fractured psyche.
Her original self was lost — only deaths remained. Countless deaths. No rebirths, just a macabre parade of flesh-vessels, each new host buckling under the weight of accumulated memories.
The sheer enormity left her with nothing but a rictus grin at the absurdity. Yet through the madness, two death-visions persisted:
Blue roses weeping dew onto thorn-strangled tombstones. Twice she witnessed this — a millennium between the viewings — yet identical down to the last petal.
When had it been? Gone now, like all things.

story.text:
In the Scarlet Vale's Secrecy Order, Durango moved as silently as his brethren.
His mask hid all expression; without so much as a whisper, this shadowed practitioner left no trace of his presence in the world.
Through rigorous study of Eastern tomes, he had forged his body into a weapon — striking with lethal precision, then vanishing like mist into darkness.

Durango spends many hours devoted to the ways of the Secrecy Order.
His freedom came at a price. The second son, he withdrew from the Sterridge family and all its internal struggles long ago.
While the family still treasure him as they always have and treat him with import, in Durango's ascetic mind, he has long been devoted to a greater cause: To see past the facades of the world and penetrate the truth.

Painstaking discipline has become a deeply ingrained in Durango's bones.
Acting with restraint has kept him from succumbing to desire, steadfastly following the path he has chosen.
Thus, unlike some of his Secrecy Order peers, Durango remains wary of contact with certain organizations, instead of forfeiting his sanity for deeper secrets.
This ascetic has always been sure of his convictions. There are no shortcuts on the path to truth.

story.text:
Journ stared intently at the experiment equipment before him, monitoring the luminosity and value of each burst of light it emitted. 
At the same time, the gnome scholar swiftly transcribed the data, his excitement impossible to contain. 
A burst of laughter escaped him, drawing a shake of the head from Follie, his niece who also worked in the same laboratory. 
"Come quick, Follie! I knew this would work!" exclaimed Journ ecstatically, before letting out a regretful sigh. It was a pity that the previous volunteer had declined to participate, or he could've witnessed this moment too.

He loves machines, particularly those powered by arcane crystals — their magic resonance magnifying the mechanisms' wonder.
To Journ, this sublime fusion of magic and machinery inspires awe no true scholar could resist.
He cares nothing beyond his experiments, retaining only the most essential knowledge.
Sometimes he even forgets his own name — a trivial detail compared to the sacred taxonomy of mineral classification.

Journ radiates perpetual joy. What scholar wouldn't, when granted the privilege of unrestrained pursuit of passion?
Even when Ergander — that kindhearted deep elf, both friend and patron — warned him of the ore-induced corruption seeping into his veins... well, such concerns found no purchase in Journ's mind.
The gnome cared not. His purpose burned singular and bright. If bearing this affliction meant swifter breakthroughs, then let the stones claim his flesh before they dull his curiosity.

story.text:
Excerpt from the libretto of the opera "Rain of Fire", Act 1: 
Lyrics: 
Woman (in pain, trembling): Neither a bird in a cage, nor a jewel in thy hand. 
Woman: I am but a timid young sprout growing from a decaying old tree. 
Woman: Bred from pestilence, a tyrant forced me to down cruel wine. 
Woman: As I grow in the freezing rain, his doctrine orders me to bloom false flowers. 
Woman: Ah, I groan, I howl. I am burned by a suffocating fire; I am minced into pieces by axes, by swords. 
Woman: Ah, I pray, I lust. I seek a power to save me, to break me free — Let my life's will be surrendered to the miraculous. 
Woman (sobbing): When will I feel thy breath, O god that I so long for?

Excerpt from the libretto of the opera "Rain of Fire", Act 2: 
Man (violently and viciously): I am the master of the land, the apex of order, the king of the herd. 
Man: The timid beastess be my feed; the unruly cubs be my sport. 
Man: They will tremble, they will worship, they will lick my fingers meek! 
Woman (gloomily): Thou art but a clown in a crumbling castle; thou art the king of rats in a narrow field of poppies. 
Man (bellowing): Beasts that covet my authority will only be trampled by me! 
Man: Shredding apart the escaping beastess, feeding her to arrogant cubs — who dares offend my glory? 
Woman (sneering): Twisted monster, disgusting insect; this be thy end. 
Woman: Behold the dark night's rain quenching the castle's flame, filling the fields of flowers with the fragrance of vengeance... 
Man (shrieking): Curse you, curse you! Wretched cubs, how can this be?! The sole king of the harbor should be I! 
Woman (smiling): Perish, be silenced, and become my puppet. I shall share with my god, the flesh and blood I be forced to eat!

Excerpt from the libretto of the opera "Rain of Fire", Act 3: 
Monster (mysterious and gentle): Ah, welcome, welcome. I am a messenger, a beacon, and I lead the worthy to bathe in glory. 
Monster: Welcome, new member. In this brilliant burning rain, let us follow our god's breath and set off for a new Elysium. 
Woman (delighted, longingly): Thou art the one who lent me strength. 
Monster: Nay, nay, that was thy own light all along. 
Woman: Thou will lead me to our god. 
Monster: Yes, yes... this nightly rain will be the final ablution.
Monster: Thy weakness, distress, and pain shall be buried by this flaming rain!

The coin bounced between Zeffi's claws and fell to the right.
The esteemed prophet grasped that coin and the revelation it contained in her palm calmly and began talking with the ratfolk who had come to her for advice.
Zeffi did not give any specific advice or guidance, only cryptic allusions.
As the chief shaman of ratfolk, she is always discreet. One does not need to divulge too much for the seed of wisdom to take root in the right mind.

Zeffi has been the longest-serving prophet of the ratfolk.
This is partly due to her extraordinary wisdom, partly because she has always guided the group without bias, and also because of the support of the ratfolk chief.
In a world that discards morality and decency, Zeffi is one of the rare beings who will make those who meet her for the first time feel the presence of peace and wisdom.

Before coming to the Hypogean District, Zeffi had lived in a human town. During a brutal pillage, her child died miserably, while she survived by hiding in a graveyard.
Grief-stricken, Zeffi left the town for the underground. She retained the habit of taking in and caring for homeless children, and one of them later became the great chief of the ratfolk.

story.text:
Lucien indifferently observed the droplets of blood trickling from the tip of his sword.
With a practiced flick of the wrist, he brought the Sword of Dawn back to rest at his side.
The surrounding populations of Increscent had long been aware of Lucien's prowess. Thus, it was often unwitting trespassers that had the audacity to test the islands' serenity.
Unfortunatately, this general wasn't an expert at letting people live, and as such, this cleanup was hardly an effective deterrent.

In his memories, his father had transformed from one concrete image into something more symbolic.
Lucien could no longer recall the daily minutiae of his longsword instruction, instead, it was replaced by his deathbed wish and the lingering smell of flames and smoke clinging to the burning building.
His father died shielding the still young prince of Thelendor, and Lucien carries on his wishes, continuing to defend this isolated island.

The general of Increscenta had long ceased to feel the stir of emotions.
Perhaps a lifetime's vigor was finite — and his had been spent in full, poured into safeguarding Increscent and the ancestral oath that weighed upon his shoulders.
Though his blood-for-blood creed found little favor among the elvenkind — not even with Lord Thelendor himself — Lucien remained unmoved.
To do right. To stand unwavering. These were never meant to be gentle paths. And so his gaze stayed fixed ahead, never turning, never yielding.

story.text:
No one had dared to approach the head of the valley recently, for terrifying thunderbolts had been raging above it. 
The thunder had gone on for so long that it even alarmed the minotaur tribe residing within the fog deep inside the valley. Cleric Schaltar asserted that this was because the clans' forbidden research had incurred the wrath of the God of Thunder, while other minotaurs believed that this was merely a one-off manifestation of the valley's treacherous and unpredictable weather. 
But it was too weird to label such weather as "natural", too — the thundering had already gone on for well over ten days, yet not a drop of rain could be seen. 
Zethos the guard, who had claimed to be patrolling atop the valley when the thunder began, was extremely excited, eagerly sharing his eyewitness account each time he bumped into someone, as if he was the central figure behind the phenomenon that was causing a stir throughout the entire valley.

"That day, I happened to accept a patrol mission. Mind you, this was my first time leaving the gate in three years! You can't imagine how tedious it is to stand guard there every day..."
"I was cautiously climbing the treacherous cliffs — yes, the ones near Riscernos's boundary, the place where scepter-wielding phantoms appear — when suddenly, the entire mountain shook. A minotaur's bellow rang out from above!"
"You heard that right, a minotaur's bellow it was! I dashed all the way to the mountaintop, and guess what I saw!"
"It was a mass of lightning as tall as a human! It was hovering in mid-air, its edges shifting constantly, just like... an accelerated version of scudding clouds! Within that mass, there was an unmoving silhouette — the profile of a minotaur! Though it had only one hoof, it was standing upright!"
"This must be a divine manifestation!"

It was clear that Zethos the minotaur had left soon after, or he would not have claimed the figure as his deity. 
... The creature behind the silhouette of the single-hoofed minotaur did not maintain it for long, and disappeared at the next lightning strike from the skies. Amidst the dust, a white figure hung diagonally across a straight pole, positioned atop the peak of the mountain at an angle incomprehensible to ordinary folks. 
The flashing lightning illuminated the figure within, revealing a mane of white hair flowing in the air. Its slightly crooked back was covered in white fur, with the arm gripping the pole spanning half its body — the creature was a white ape! 
He gazed motionlessly at the distant clouds. After a long pause, he let out a soft sigh. 
"It's time to go, Kui."
