story.text:
"Indeed," Adolphus scoffed, shaking his head, "there's a fair few who believe themselves better qualified to treat these wounds and curses than I... And certainly, that's one opinion."
He shook his head, turning his back on the deep elf trying to detain him. This treatment was cut short.
"But, I seldom saw any of them afterwards. That's good, isn't it? For both of us."

Adolphus had studied the healing arts out of mere interest. As a noble, he never needed to subsist on it.
As for the rest of the Unyielding Silk's deep elf nobility, every one of them was suspicious, loathing and terrified of other nobles. How could they possibly ask him to attend to them?
They couldn't be more inclined to conceal every weakness, revealing only their immaculate surfaces.
Yet for all Adolphus' healing prowess, his gifts found little practical application.

Curiously, healing arts and spells share more in common than one might think — often they're two sides of the same coin.
This revelation crowned Adolphus' years of research. He delighted in its duality: a metaphysical pun with deadly serious implications.
Though he occasionally tested his theories, he limited his subjects to outsiders. However little love he bore for the deep elves, he knew better than to stage grotesque experiments in the Spider Mother's domain.

story.text:
Soveliss stood around the Driftwood's coast, letting waves flush his bare feet.
Since his coming here, he often stood here for a whole day. The islands of this archipelago scattered in a distance, leaving only their vague outline in the mist.
However, Aethercairn was not his homeland.
Soveliss knew he couldn't see Nytheria from here, let alone their holy tree. What annoyed him most was that he could rarely see the lush forest even in his dream.

He was an escapee.
But anyway, the Blue Oak was going to die, and the once flourishing Swaddling Forest became an evil and highly polluted place. This forest was not able to feed the whole wood elf tribe anymore.
There must be someone making a decision.
Before leading his tribespeople away, Soveliss bid farewell to his brother Ivellios at the Surka River's ferry.
He promised he would return to Nytheria one day. However, he had no idea if that was to come true.

On the journey to Aethercairn, Soveliss' son was born amidst the shimmering waves of the open sea.
In later years, he would sometimes wonder if this had been a sign from Nythurys, an ineffable boundary drawn between the new and the old.
As years passed, Yfeir grew like a young sapling, and like many elves of his generation, he did not cling to the Blue Oak's protection as the elders did.
But Soveliss was different. He remained a relic of bygone days, shaped by Nythurys' radiance. When all is said and done, he hopes only to return to the embrace of the Grand Cycle at life's end.

story.text:
Embers spat as Eli fed another branch to the fire.
The one-eyed mercenary exhaled sharply, his back finding purchase against a gnarled root. After a beat of consideration, he slid his crossbow closer — close enough to kiss.
Windsper Forest kept its rare silence. Unlike the clamor of towns, this suited the lone sellsword just fine. Human voices set his teeth on edge. Only in true solitude did peace ever settle upon his shoulders.

Eli has always believed that all beings in the world change in their journey of growth. Whether good or ill, it's always a departure from naivety.
As a man who has experienced dramatic change, the word "naïve" has long ceased to resonate with Eli.
Incidentally, he now finds himself at a complete loss owing to the kindness showered upon him by a certain Athalean wood elf lass. Especially since she's so young. In wood elf terms, she's merely an innocent girl, and a very long life yet awaits her.

In Eli's homeland, he is a sinner.
But it's not the sin that matters. What matters is the change to his status. Once you're branded a sinner, you're an outcast, albeit in mentality alone. They won't welcome you in. On the bright side, despite being cast out of his home, he can still fill his stomach thanks to his mastery of the crossbow. But he just can't work as a team. Trusting others? He's far too wary. Fortunately, that's hardly a big problem.
In Nytheria, the trees swallow histories whole. Just walk deep enough, and your past becomes just another leaf in the wind.

story.text:
The lantern cast a violet glow, its eerie light pulsing faintly through the darkness as Zadok swung his arm.
The specters summoned by its power radiated the same unnatural chill, warding off malevolent spirits that haunted the City of the Dead. Even in death, the law remained: kill or be devoured.
Zadok shrugged. This truth had governed all existence since long before his first breath.

In life, Zadok served as a centurion of the Dragonsaerie Imperial Army. Even after death, he upholds his armor-clad stance.
Yet, despite being accustomed to using swords and axes, Zadok now feels more at home wielding summoning magic, eschewing some of his old habits.
Fear rattles him on occasion: Death brings irreversible change, but what remains if these changes go on in perpetuity? What's left?

To choose military service was to embrace death's inevitability.
Zadok had never expected to be among the lucky survivors. Nor had he foreseen how abruptly the end would come, severing him from his wife and their newborn daughter.
Throughout his imprisonment in the City of the Dead, he had strained toward the capital upon those golden plains.
The dead know no true sleep. Yet in rare moments of weariness, Zadok would still glimpse his daughter's small hand reaching for his vanished right arm.

story.text:
Iola is fond of the Scarlet Vale's Great Library.
Unlike most wizards studying here, she's not a quiet sort that has her head buried in ancient tomes. The wizards that make the journey here are not only those of the Vale. There are those wise ones who hail from the outside world, and have undergone trials to finally arrive here.
Iola enjoys speaking with them. These little chats are not without merit, allowing her to learn new things on occasion.

The more one plumbs the depths of wisdom, the more one's opinions lean towards the vitriolic and obstinate.
Iola has met too many such wizards. Once every few decades, nightly talks are held in the Great Library, and with frequency they devolve from hushed debates into bitter arguments.
This is where she shines. Her intelligent, polished discourse stills the stormy waters, ushering the evening's wisdom back in.

People paint Iola as silver-tongued and eloquent, but it is just one side of her.
In truth, this wizard is just as spectacularly paranoid and fanatical as the peers she often soothes and pacifies. She just happens to be good at hiding it, not exposing it in her day-to-day chatter.
To sup from the fount of knowledge is akin to sipping wine, and despite her intoxication, Iola maintains her habitual sipping. In her opinion, this is the only way to make it last.

story.text:
"Inferno" Caraman has a bit of a reputation amongst adventurers. With a fierce and frightful visage and a flaming weapon, he has successfully tackled numerous challenging commissions, which has cemented his standing as a trusted and skilled adventurer. 
However, there are dissenters who argue that his accomplishments are merely a facade. They claim that when faced with formidable enemies, he would always be the first one to flee, and that this skill was precisely what allowed him to be the sole survivor in every single party he joined, enabling him to conceal the true circumstances that went on and claim credit for his teammates' achievements. 
As for whether this is true, it would be best to clarify with Caraman himself.

Caraman remains optimistic and undisturbed by such rumors, for he is well aware of his own limitations. 
Apart from his unusual appearance caused by a particular incident, he has no exceptional qualities and is no different from an ordinary human being. Even with his abundant adventuring experience, he knows that it cannot guarantee his safety in every situation. 
Thus, he dedicated himself to honing his escape skills. To his surprise, he seemed to have an innate instinct for sensing danger. As a seasoned adventurer who has managed to stay alive and be relatively unscathed to this day, he considers himself very fortunate. 
Regarding the rumors of him abandoning his teammates... Well, Caraman would always dutifully warn his teammates when they were no match for their upcoming enemies, and always obtained approval before he retreated each time — albeit with disdainful remarks from his team that he needn't follow if he was afraid. Caraman could only shrug at their response. After all, it was impossible to force anyone who had no intention of escaping to do so.

Only once did Caraman defy his sense for danger. He had been too young at that time, so under the confident guidance of his senior, he forcefully suppressed his gut instincts of doubt and followed him deep into the cave. There, they encountered undead that were undefeatable. 
In the end, only a disfigured Caraman survived the ordeal, bringing back his senior's ashes with him. "RUN!" was his senior's last words to him, before he perished and had his body consumed by flames. 
Caraman buried his senior's ashes, and came to terms with his hideously cursed face that burned forevermore. 
In his subsequent adventures, whenever his instincts kicked in, he would always warn everyone before danger approached — "RUN!".

story.text:
"Nothing over here, check over there."
"Yessir!"
The men saluted Captain Gareth and headed off to continue the search for deserters.
A suspicious rustling was heard in the bushes beside them. Gareth sighed quietly, reining in his restless mount — he knew the deserter, Lorarii, was hiding right there. Gareth narrowly diverted his men's attention this time, but he couldn't be sure of next time.
"This really isn't a good spot." Gareth mumbled, as if to himself, "I understand not being able to hack it. But this is where my help ends. I wish you luck in getting wherever it is you're going."
With those words, Gareth whirled his horse about and rode away.

Gareth had never imagined life could offer other paths.
The swing of a blade, the knife-edged winds howling through watchtower beams, the bone-white snows of Canine Peak — these were his world. Dragonsaerie and the Knight Order of Platinum might as well have been fireside tales. But not all men shared his knack for swallowing fate like stale bread.
He understood why that knight chose to flee. The frontier's bloody grind and lean years weren't for every stomach. Yet in some hidden corner of his heart, embers still glowed — a stubborn hope for kinder shores where all of them might yet wash up.

That assault was a turning point.
The might of the orcs had exceeded all of their expectations. He watched his longtime comrades perish miserably, run through by orc weapons. He watched as Wolf Keep, stood in silence for centuries, was lost to those savages. He watched as, for the first time, the flag of the Empire retreated east of the Old Highlands.
A fate that looms over us all approaches, he realized.
But until then, he was still captain of the Knight Order of Dragon Blood, and he would wield the sword in his hand to the bitter end.

story.text:
Gardrus coughed loudly, sputtering his ale all over the table.
Sounds of discontent rumbled around him, but he was far too drunk to comprehend it. His tawny red beard looked pitiful soaked in booze and dappled vomit.
The moment patrol was over, the dwarf would race to his favorite haunt, the tavern, and drink until the crack of dawn.
As for tomorrow's work, Gardrus had long cast it from his mind.

Much like his older brother, he has no interest in engaging his brain.
If they can hold their weapons, they're useful fortress guards. Anything beyond that takes too much thought — it's just a headache.
They've been long in this job, no longer youngsters, but they don't care for it. It's just gold in their purses.
And naturally, that gold is frittered away on booze and women.

The two brothers, Gardrus and Thurnus, live together.
The house isn't a grand affair. Gardrus being somewhat untidy, and his brother being equally unkempt, often leads to fights over who should be cleaning this week.
Amidst the bickering, the better paid older sibling always uses his seniority to rebuke Gardrus.
The tedium of fraternal squabbling seems never-ending, and the dwarves even take some pleasure in it.

story.text:
Sometimes, Kamari wonders if his 18-year-old self who made the vow to become a paladin could have foreseen such a day. 
Around him, there are no warm, beautiful houses, nor cheers from an adoring crowd, but only the unrelenting storms of Canine Peak and the menacing eyes of the orc tribe. 
He harbors no regrets for his decision, but when he sees the young and confused faces of his soldiers, he questions if it was worth paying such a high price for it all.

"Arbortea is a monster that devours people." That was what a village elder warned this young boy before he set off for Dragonsaerie.
At that time, Kamari didn't fully comprehend the meaning of those words.
It wasn't until the platinum knights held him down and forced him to kneel and confess to false crimes before the chief wizard that he truly understood the significance of that warning.

He seeks revenge. 
Not against the empire that abandoned him, but against all the wickedness, the shameless conspiracies, and the other deeds that have led innocents to their deaths. 
If those with malicious intentions wish to interpret his vow as an act of rebellion, then so be it. He has already hit rock bottom and has nothing left to lose. 
But from the beginning until the very end, his heart, body, and mind — everything will all belong to the empire. That will never change.

story.text:
Isitarian still remembers the era when people worshiped the Dragon God. 
Back then, everything had been governed by the rules set by the Dragon God, and mortal hearts were pure, and every god knew their place. Until one day, someone, called the Child of Chaos, appeared out of nowhere and disrupted the stability, invading with a black mist from the Outlands that engulfed the once peaceful world. 
But the world needed order — that was Isitarian's understanding from the beginning, and he couldn't fathom why anyone would deliberately destroy everything. 
Regardless, he remained the most devout follower of the Mother of Dragons, and he was willing to do whatever it took to protect her order.

He couldn't understand how he could have made such a mistake. 
After all these years, he should have already become familiar with all his responsibilities. He had once led an order of nearly ten thousand, and had thus been honored with the role of the keeper of the Mother of Dragons' residence. 
However, he committed an act of negligence — the devout and cautious Isitarian who had never once slipped up relaxed the barrier to the Mother of Dragons' residence, allowing the Child of Chaos and his subordinates to penetrate deep inside. 
As he watched the Child of Chaos stand before the Dragon Queen, he knew in his heart that there was no way to make up for the mistake he had made.

Isitarian harbored no hatred — not even when the Dragon Queen herself cast him into the prison-realms of Chaos Universum.
He understood his sins were unforgivable. He knew her punishments were just. He saw, too, how her every act served some grand design.
The Mother of Dragons was truth incarnate: the world’s foundation, its creatures’ breath. None dared question her will. And so Isitarian clung to faith — that if he remained devout, she who had exiled him would one day restore him.
This conviction never faltered.

story.text:
Dane read the parchment's scriptures, his sunken eyes blinking, a hint of madness flashing through them.
He had already been enthralled by these doctrines. Of course they were so enlightening — Why were there always fools who could not understand these truths?!
He was filled with unjustified anger for a moment, but in the next, Dane's brows relaxed.
It was fine, the true god would only forgive pious followers — just let those fools' souls perish with this world.

Dane stuffed a stack of yellowing parchment into the hands of the urchin, "Go, deliver these letters filled with truths to passersby, and you'll get a bag of delicious candies."
The child, trusting his words, complied but later found no trace of the mysteriously robed man.
"For the sake of this world's absolution, what deceptions should not be made? These lies serve but to further a noble cause — for the god demands more followers, countless followers!" Dane always told himself.

Dane was once a prosperous merchant wealthy beyond measure, with handsome looks that turned many heads.
But good times never lasted long — the fortunes obtained through irregular means soon brought great trouble to Dane.
In the dead of night, a mysterious fire broke out, consuming everyone in silence.
The fire destroyed Dane's appearance, but gave his mind and soul an opportunity for rebirth. A dark-cloaked stranger saved Dane, extending an invitation: "Behold this corrupt world that has wronged you — would you not see those responsible eradicated?"

story.text:
Gladros heard the faint clatter of his scales against armor. He trembled violently, his body beyond control.
This was his first battle.
Every drill vanished from his mind. Blank-eyed, he missed his companions’ mocking stares. "I’ll die first," he thought desperately.
Courage... Where does it even grow?
A guttural war cry startled him. The advancing blades intensified his panic. With a shriek, he jabbed his spear blindly.
He kept stabbing and stabbing, until cold blood streaked his armor. Only when no blades remained did Gladros snap back to awareness.
He’d survived.

Teasing Gladros was endlessly entertaining. The faintest rustle of grass would send him leaping in panic, limbs flailing as his tail thrashed against the ground.
People said he stayed a soldier only out of fear for his father. Born to a warrior lineage, he had endured brutal training since childhood — destined for battlefields his timid soul loathed.
Yet the mockers overlooked one truth: Pitiful Gladros survived. Campaign after campaign, he emerged alive.

Gladros loathed his cowardice.
It was unbecoming. Shameful. A sin.
Yet control eluded him. Beneath the armor, his body shook with tremors known only to him. How he longed to flee — from his father’s scorn, from the jeering crowds, to some forgotten corner where he could curl alone around his terror.
But he stayed. Duty demanded it. Though fear turned his bones to water, he fought. Again and again, he survived.
That stubborn duty burned brighter than any warrior’s courage.

story.text:
Joyce stared into the mirror. 
"Is this a mirror, or a puddle of water? Which would reflect my soul more clearly? Wait... but which soul?" 
He drew back the corners of his painted mouth, and his reflection stared back at him with a mournful expression. 
"Oh! Oh! No, not 'this' me..." Joyce felt a surge of ecstasy, before being pierced by a burst of sorrow. 
"Which is me?!" He asked aloud to his other self, but only silence greeted him.

He is an outstanding star performer in the Hysteria Troupe. 
Joyce always manages to win applause from the crowd with his exaggerated performances, with playing multiple roles as his specialty. 
He is able to go from weeping bitterly to laughing uproariously in an instant. But what the audience doesn't know is that beneath Joyce's turbulent display, there is a soul in turmoil. 
Joyce is aware of the many individuals who exist within his body — there exist many versions of himself, many performers, and many Joyces...

Joyce loved talking to himself.
Few understood this — least of all the daylight crowd, those mundane souls drowning in life’s chores. But the night cultivated finer audiences, and performers needed only follow the troupe’s caravan.
Why seek others when I remain my own greatest mystery? If self-knowledge was this elusive, why waste breath on strangers’ shallow depths?
So Joyce let his fractured selves spill outward, pooling into sentient shadows. At last — clarity.

story.text:
Lethander reviewed the documents once more.
Some were letters — letters from informants, letters from converts. Fascinating, truly, that deep elves couldn't trust one another but were inclined to keep track of these things.
Their readiness to keep records was a boon, providing more information to help him make wiser decisions.
But Lethander wasn't one for talking, especially when General Quaesitia had already passed her own verdict.

He had been Quaesitia's chief advisor for many years.
Handling this domineering general was no mean feat. Luckily for Lethander, he had enough wisdom to justify his existence, and since he could demonstrate that wisdom at the appropriate moments, he had maintained his role as advisor for a very long time.
Precious little could escape Lethander's notice — his web of spies blanketed the city, silken and suffocating.

Lethander handled many affairs for his general, and it served him well enough.
Granted, he had to mind his tongue to ensure his survival, after all, he'd already witnessed many a loquacious deep elf meet a fate worse than death — all because they'd violated the boundaries of the general's power.
Still, Lethander would dare pipe up at certain moments and persuade Quaesitia to rethink her decisions. He is one of the scant few who can do this and live to see another day.

story.text:
Questa toyed with her serrated cutlass, lips curling into a venomous grin.
Blood oozed down the blade’s barbed edge, dripping from her fingers onto the corpse of her recent employer — the same man who’d hired her mere hours ago.
Pity he talked too much and paid too little, she mused. Now she’d have to interrogate that merchant caravan he’d wanted dead — maybe they’d have better jobs on offer.

Questa has an exceptionally awful reputation with the criminal underworld around Aquitaine.
As well as deriving great pleasure in torture, her volatile nature is a nuisance, and it is impossible to gauge what she will do on a whim. This frenemy approach makes everyone who deals with Questa extremely wary.
A gorgeous but crazy femme fatale. That's what malcontents say.

When Questa was nine years old, the merchant caravan that took her in was wiped out by the Wolfspider, a bandit gang.
The young girl joined the bandits, and killed the leader who laid claim to her not long after, along with slaughtering the old gang members. She then established a new bandit gang.
On occasions when the Wolfspider leader she murdered is mentioned, Questa dispassionately calls him her dead husband, and father.
Morality and principles are far removed from her sphere. She has only one rule: no killing girls under the age of ten. She knows of her infamy, but she couldn't care less.

story.text:
When that person reached out to him, he had already become a tortured and broken shell. 
He never thought that he would have any kind of future — this continent had never favored him. From his birth to his impending death, he was only a puppet that disaster and malice swallowed, then spat out. 
But that person appeared before him, and asked if he was willing to change everything with him. 
That person called Himself the Child of Chaos.

The ritual to become an Unstill was long and painful, but it was nothing compared to the hardship that he had experienced in his early life. 
When he opened his eyes once again, the Child of Chaos, the person who had become his new master, stood before him, smiling. 
He told Voresh that he was now a being beyond the grasp of life and death, and none of his old shackles could ever restrain him again. He asked if Voresh would pledge loyalty to him, and join him in carrying out his grand scheme to overthrow everything. 
Voresh kneeled, trembling, and kissed his toes.

They failed, vanquished by the overwhelming power of the Mother of Dragons.
And the Child of Chaos — his master, his savior, his everything — was thrown into the strongest of cages and plunged into a long and endless sleep.
But everything is not over yet, for he knows that his existence is for this very moment. He would give up everything for his master. In the face of his goal, killing a thousand innocent exiles, or even sacrificing his own soul, means nothing.
Their grand scheme will succeed in the end, and he is more convinced of this fact than anyone else.

story.text:
Isolde cocked her head out of habit.
There was nobody around anymore. Only now did she rouse from her fleeting daze. In the past, the place was alive with bustle. The mercenary band was full of people of every pedigree, and sometimes people laughed, but more frequently, they quarreled over all manner of pettiness.
But now, they were all gone. It was difficult to adjust at first, but she came to accept it as the years rolled by.

She'd once been a member of Adenthia's prestigious mercenary cadre, as well as a favorite guest of many a prominent figure.
However, they ought to have realized that it never ends well to dabble too deeply in affairs of authority. That Dragonsaerie Regent's request lit the fuse of their demise.
Of course, Isolde knew that they had been falsely accused, but not a soul would believe it.

Seeking a resolution, Isolde embarked on a journey.
Being a lone wolf was very different from acting as a unit, with many things proving more troublesome to deal with. There were times she had to compromise on her reward, but she never considered giving up.
Until she found the one responsible for framing them, Isolde would continue prowling around in the dead of night, right until she sank her teeth into their throat.
Every once in a while, she'd wish for a place to belong once more, like the mercenary band of her past, but those thoughts were fleeting beside the drive for vengeance.

story.text:
Frurbath wandered through the dense forests of Nytheria. 
The troll was searching for some rare herbs for Boss Oggok, even though they were difficult to find — some of them grew in precarious locations, or came from dangerous sources. 
Frurbath muttered under his breath as he reached out to pull apart a thick growth of plants. He hoped to be back before the rain, because that, combined with the humid environment of the forest, was perilous.

Few trolls can understand what Frurbath says when he talks. 
After a long period of teaching, even Oggok acknowledged that his subordinate truly lacked linguistic ability. To this day, Frurbath still speaks like a newborn baby, and muttering disjointed and fractured words is all he can do. 
Luckily, fate has not abandoned him completely — his talent for witchcraft surpasses that of the other trolls, allowing him to survive in the tribe.

Frurbath worships his chieftain Oggok, treating the witchdoctor's every word as divine law.
When Oggok resolved to lead their tribe from Mog-Nach to Nytheria's shadowed woods, Frurbath stood among the first loyal followers.
Right or wrong, Witchdoctor Oggok or Chief Trolgar — these questions never troubled Frurbath's mind. His loyalty belongs solely to the one who taught him witchcraft. As for complexities, he'd leave them to cleverer trolls to ponder about!

story.text:
Garius staggered forward drunkenly.
His pike swung in wild, uncontrolled arcs.
He no longer knew who — or what — he fought. The battlefield around him had blurred into a meaningless haze.
The bronze mask clung to his face like a leech, its grip relentless. His own thoughts faded, replaced entirely by the mask's commands.

While the wizards of the Vale aren't overly fond of engaging with the world outside, that doesn't mean they're averse to plumbing its recesses for secrets.
Garius had dealt with them plenty of times before. Being an employed outsider, he knew that these eccentric types always wound up finding obscure treasure caches.
Of course, he wouldn't take any extra — it was just hard won dues, and the wizard's rewards weren't anything to write home about.
Garius' single most damning act of avarice, was slipping that mask out of the cache.

Remorse festered in Garius' chest.
True lucidity came rarely — most often, that grotesque mask held him in thrall, reducing him to a shambling corpse.
Only in fleeting moments did his body's control return to him.
He longed to cry for help, to voice his torment, yet every attempt died half-spoken on his lips.
That mask... whose face had it once covered? He knew not. He knew only this: his pike-work surpassed all past skill, and with each dawn... the battle-hunger gnawed deeper.

story.text:
A night owl landed on Irma's head. Thinking a huge curved horn of the halfling's helmet a tree branch, it sat itself upon it for a moment's pause, before screeching gruffly, ruffling its wings, and taking to the skies.
Irma chuckled soundlessly. During night vigil, such amusing interludes often transpired.
Lurking amidst the mountains, blanketed by midnight's shadows, she becomes one with nature. Birds settle on her head, and critters scamper beside the shores of her feet. The halfling's bright, keen eyes are ever vigilant, observing all around, alert to anything that may threaten the tranquility of Eulestein.

Stanguem's double-sickle guards the day in Eulestein, and Irma's bow and arrow watch over the night.
Irma has quietly dealt with miscreants trying to sneak in many times. Unlike Stanguem's loud warning drums, she prefers to deal with these small problems alone, without disturbing the peaceful sleep of her fellow inhabitants.
She is much friendlier to outlanders than Stanguem. But all the villains who attempted to take advantage of that friendliness had a deadly arrow stuck in their throats. She does not object to their chief's innovative ideas. The technology provided by those outlanders makes her arrows sharper, providing a more direct benefit compared to the manageable risks within her control.

Irma’s endless nights began with an ambush.
Orcish war cries shattered the mountain’s peace, staining a trembling child’s vision crimson.
She lost everything that night — parents, home, the fragile comfort of safety. Since then, darkness has refused to grant her eyelids respite.
So she wielded that fear like a weapon, transforming into the clan’s shadowed sentinel.
Only at dawn, wrapped in sunlight and birdsong, does she finally find solace — eyes closing with the quiet triumph of a people kept safe through the night.

story.text:
Eches rises on her toes, her body undulating with the haunting melody.
Eyes shut tight, she has shed all memory of self and place. Nothing exists but the glorious symphony around her — each rhythm birthing the next, each step flowing into another.
Deep in Nytheria's untrodden woods, Eches dances alone. No audience gathers for this performance. These steps are no mere art... but the silent tuning of a killing instrument.

Eches wears the thief's mantle — but not its conventions.
Behind her mask dwells a woman who plays by no rules but her own. For her, the artistry of the act matters as much as the prize.
And of all death's many faces, she's chosen dance as its perfect partner. Let the dying protest; she'll still gift each soul a final waltz, her blades keeping time with their fading heartbeats.

She has completely forgotten the first time she saw that dance.
Indeed, what she witnessed was not a dance, but the final throes of a struggle before death.
In her burning village, plundered by thieves, that was the last sight the girl beheld. Those confined to the houses flailed their arms and swung their legs as scorching flames reduced them to black char.
In a frenzied panic, Eches fled to the dense woods, never to return.

story.text:
Throughout the course of time, Vicuc couldn't recall how many of his fellows he'd farewelled. The elderly, his peers, children that died too young. He doesn't fear perishing, he placidly trusts: All souls shall return to the Grand Cycle — even if the Grand Cycle has been obstructed for millennia.
To reinitiate the cycle once more, Vicuc volunteered his life in sacrifice. He pushed doubt to the back of his mind, electing to trust his dear friend's judgment and the revelations of Nythurys.
Vicuc smiled, nodding his head lightly in greeting to his dear friend one last time as he ascended the altar.
Then...
Then what...?

Three centuries are no fleeting span, even for the long-lived wood elves.
With each passing year, fewer remain who remember the old days. To the younger generations, Vicuc has ever been but a morose recluse, frail and forgotten.
High Priestess Jathalea's deliberate indifference became a silent decree, turning their kin's respect for the elder into wary distance.
In the days when his limbs still obeyed him, Vicuc would labor each dawn toward the Cemetery of No-Return. There he stood, eyes fixed on the distant Altar of the Withering, whispering words only the wind could catch.
His bent frame seemed to carry the weight of all wood elf souls denied by the Grand Cycle's embrace, their collective sorrow made manifest in his trembling steps.

In a past purposely shunned, Vicuc was once the deacon of a wood elf clan. Ivellios, the high priest, was his dear friend, and Jathalea was their remarkable successor.
They received a revelation from the forest, and performed the ritual in accordance, hoping to renew the lost Grand Cycle once more...
But, the ritual failed. Ivellios vanished, the three altars were corrupted, and the forest was rendered a murky domain infested with Sylvan Furies.
Vicuc never again saw Ivellios, thus was never afforded the reason why he interrupted the ritual that day. In the midst of unresolved bewilderment and frustration, he grew older by the day.
If he cannot be answered, even after death, he'll just keep languishing, won't he...?

story.text:
The door that had been closed for a long time was finally pulled open from the inside. Estella walked out of the sickroom gracefully, handing the wooden box she was holding to the maid.
"He's fine now. Don't forget my payment."
The patient's relative nodded carefully, eyes full of awe and gratitude.
Rumor has it that Estella was proficient in mysterious healing techniques, able to heal rotten, bare-boned wounds, reattach severed limbs, and even revive the dead.
No one knew what methods she used exactly, but each time, she would charge a high price — a jar of fresh blood from a living person, filled to the brim.

Estella was born into the Ptolemies. As the most favored little daughter, she grew up under the protection of her elders.
Everything she wanted seemed within easy reach, but there was a rule in the family that the east wing of the library was strictly off limits.
Perhaps out of curiosity, or childhood rebelliousness, she sneaked into the forbidden area. There didn't seem to be anything unusual here. Just as she was about to leave out of boredom, she was drawn to a bookshelf, grasping a book spine sealed by golden symbols.
As the pages flipped open before her eyes, the ancient, mysterious characters seeped into her mind like poison. The sudden, intense headache sent Estella into a coma lasting several months. When she opened her eyes again, the innocence in them was gone.

Estella walked around the sickbed holding a pricket, and the flames suddenly turned an eerie purple. Looking at the unconscious patient in bed, she smiled.
The dagger etched with the family crest quietly sliced open the patient's chest. She watched calmly and coldly as his life drained away. When the patient's heartbeat stopped completely, she took the medicine bottle that had been sitting on the table and poured it into the corpse's mouth.
The flames on the pricket turned back to a warm orangey-red. Before her eyes, the wounds healed at a visible speed. Estella closed the medicine box satisfied — the research had progressed smoothly this time.

story.text:
Chaos gifted Zhar’loth an eye.
A violet eye. An unblinking eye. An all-seeing eye.
With this eye, no other senses were needed.
He saw the drip of water, heard the guttural snarls of his kin as visible sound, witnessed the hungry pulse of embryos craving nourishment from warm flesh. Envy festered. Instinct took over — he lunged —
Then came the crimson warmth. Blood splashed across the staring orb embedded in his chest, flooding his clouded mind with vengeance’s sweet rapture.

Zhar'loth is nothing but an eye embedded in a writhing mass of flesh. 
By the Fallen Souls' rough allocation of duties, he drifts about the great embryo, protecting his gestating kin, on alert to eliminate potential threats. Nothing is concealed from his gaze: with the blessing of Chaos growing with each passing day, his eye only becomes brighter, glinting in the darkness. 
Everything is reflected in this eye. 
Yet there is only darkness within it.

The ancient annals of the deep elves still contain trace records of the origins of Fallen Souls. They had been exiled into the darkest depths of the Tainted Tower due to a madness that arose from reasons unknown. 
Zhar'loth was one amongst those who had been caught up in the frenzy. He had always felt like the Underground was way too dark to see anything, even for the eyes of a deep elf. 
And thus, on that very day, he discovered that he had gained an additional eye. 
This eye allowed him to see the ugliness of his kin, the twistedness within himself, and everything lurking in the dark that should have never been seen. He descended into agony and madness, yet he was never able to close that eye again. He watched as his kin and his own body became distorted by depravity; he watched as his former brethren enacted cruel banishments; he watched everything... and his hatred grew. 
One day, he would watch them all perish in misery.

story.text:
With his face hidden behind a mask, Vasska no longer remembers how he looks. 
He has no thoughts of his own, and simply listens to the voice in silence. 
The voice resembles notes of some musical instrument, yet sounds so silent — it carries a concealed madness, echoing within his chest and skull.
The voice of his deity rises higher and higher, turning even louder, huskier, and more silent...

Death was only just a beginning, and Vasska had already crossed that boundary. However, there were no limits to the other side of that boundary — at the root of nothingness was chaos. 
He had forgotten everything from his past life, or rather, he no longer recalled it. 
If his master so desired, he would summon those memories once again. If not, they simply ceased to exist. 
The existence of the world itself was not exactly real, but the people in it remained unaware of this fact.

Vasska, concealed in his black robes, silently carries out the elder's tasks. 
He is naturally subservient, and obeys the elder's every command. As an agent of chaos, he had no other choice but to obey. 
An Unstill — this term does not precisely define what he is; only the master of this world truly knows what the Unstill are. 
They are the keys tucked away in the shadows of this world, and the one who can open the lock has not yet returned. 
But the wait wouldn't be long now. Soon... very soon.

story.text:
Lydia relishes the vanilla-laced firewine of Dragonsaerie Tavern.
Each dusk, when the village caravan's gold is safely stowed, she claims her usual perch — that absurdly tall stool no halfling could scale without a running start — flashes the barkeep a grin sharp as her old dagger, and downs a half-cask of the blazing spirit.
In years past, the weight of those coin-heavy pouches invited trouble. Thrice a night, some fool might test her.
Then came the revelation: she traded her blade for a gnarled cudgel, its knotted bulk now planted before her tankard like a warning totem. Not a soul has dared approach since.

Lydia's second favorite drink is a fine forest wine from a distant forest. 
She once yearned to journey to far-off lands and even accepted invitations from mercenary teams to travel into dense forests, snowy mountains, or perpetually scorching deserts. 
Lydia honed her skills through the countless battles she fought, with her choice of weapon increasing in size, and her nickname evolving from "Little Wino" to "Drunken Dame". 
However, at every celebratory feast filled with the aroma of wine, Lydia would always feel a little lost. 
Drinking for the gold she had earned, drinking for the accomplishments she had achieved, drinking to help a young wizardess beat up her cheating man— 
But aren't there surely happier reasons to drink?

Lydia's favorite wine is still the specialty fruit wine from Uerus. 
When she was still a little girl, she would routinely climb onto the wine barrel and steal a drink amidst the revelry of the Harvest Festival. 
On her 25th Harvest Festival, Lydia returned to her hometown late at night after another journey only to find several drunken children at the doorstop of her house. 
As she gazed upon their faces, the fruity winds blowing against their cheeks, the wandering warrior slung her weapon on her shoulder, finally finding her reason to raise her glass.

story.text:
Corrin meticulously inspected the traveler's belongings before finally waving them through with a frown.
The recent influx of outsiders to Eulestein sat ill with him — a troubling trend, without doubt. In an ideal world, he'd bar every last stranger at the gates. Yet the Reformers' influence left him no choice.
So he stood his watch, protecting the sanctuary of ridge halflings in his own way. If he couldn't keep them all out, he'd filter out the wolves slinking among the sheep.

Unlike his brother Lyle, who shunned the Reformers completely, Corrin had once attempted to infiltrate their ranks.
Not that he'd ever wavered in his convictions — this was merely a different tactic to dismantle their alliance from within.
Yet the gambit failed in the end.
What emerged was a Corrin transformed: harder, sharper, more unyielding than even the staunchest traditionalists, which prompted many of the village elders to join him.

Corrin and Lyle lost their parents during an orc invasion.
An entirely preventable accident — though Corrin would argue "trap" were the apter term.
All because their parents trusted the merchants who often came to the village. Such impulsiveness claimed their lives.
The ridge halflings have their own way of life, dealing with outsiders only leads to disaster. It doesn't make sense to Corrin that so many of his brethren can't grasp that!

story.text:
The man clutched his drink, eyes beneath his hood peering around warily: A few tables of raucous commoners fresh from work, two regulars flirting with the barmaid, and a drunken dwarf, who, half-asleep, raised his head from the table, pulled money clumsily from his pocket, slapped it in the owner's hand to pay the bill, and staggered out the door.
Nothing remarkable. The man lowered his guard and bowed his head to knock back his drink. These past few days spent fugitive have taken their toll on this privileged former official. Seducing a young lady and running off was quite a misstep. Grimly he thought, not only had he failed at blending in with the gentry, but the lord had put out a call for his life.
Suddenly, the sharp sound of glass breaking, and the cool sensation across his temples halted the man's train of thought. The other patrons began to scream. Instinctively, the man raised his hand to feel: A crossbow bolt, penetrating his head from left through to right.
Anger gone, his head slammed onto the table with a resounding thud, smashing the plates and scattering bowls. The dwarf who'd made his exit just a short while ago deftly vaulted through the window, nodding with satisfaction.
"One off the list. "

Theodore was a dwarf, and an unnervingly shrewd mercenary at that. Savvy, after all, wasn't a trait one typically associated with his kin.
His prices were steep, his terms inflexible: no credit, no haggling, profit maximized to the last copper. Many saw him as ruthlessly pragmatic... Never stood a round of drinks, and by the beard — the dwarf didn't even touch ale! What sort of dwarf was that?
Yet none could deny his record: not a single contract botched. However vile or vexing the task, if Theodore took the job, satisfaction was guaranteed.
For wealthy patrons who preferred clean results over empty promises, he remained, quite simply, a "great choice" in the business.

"The Great Choice" Theodore treasured but one thing above all — his crossbow.
This weathered companion had put food on his table for decades. After every contract, without fail, he'd disassemble, clean, and oil each component with ritualistic care.
So long as the weapon sang true, coins kept flowing. None knew what became of the fortunes earned through blood and thrift — that dream he cradled closer than any dwarven ancestral relic. Some secrets weren't meant for sharing.
Yet for this sole indulgence, no expense was spared. Even the shrewdest dwarf knows where true value lies. And Theodore? He always makes the best choice.

story.text:
"My comrades are all dead... and I..."
As the orc's battleaxe descended, Elvis let his shield fall, only a faint whisper of defiance left in him. Torrents of blood carried away his consciousness, the pain fading into death's embrace.
He awoke to a frozen hell. Entombed in ice among the corpses, he stirred — and the scavenging hounds turned their hungry eyes upon him.
Elvis rose. His body bore no weight, no scent, no pain. Only ghosts spoke now:
"Hey, Elvis! Ale’s waiting at the tavern!"
"Gods, this heat’ll boil us alive... Must we drill tomorrow?"
Then — the axe came again. This time, his shield arm held steady.

Elvis’ upbringing held little worthy of song.
A commoner’s firstborn, he’d silently shield his younger brother from neighborhood bullies, taking their blows without complaint. A guardsman — moved by the boy’s stoicism — intervened. Thereafter, he entrusted Elvis with errands, letting him earn some coins honestly.
One day, that guardsman fell to a cutpurse’s dagger. Small but quick, Elvis latched onto the thief’s leg like a barnacle on a hull, buying crucial moments. When reinforcements arrived, they discovered the boy bore three knife wounds to his back... without a single whimper.
Thus did Elvis of Dragonsaerie earn his place in the Dragonsaerie army.

As long as he remained on this blood-soaked battlefield, Elvis could hear his comrades' voices.
He tried to follow the source of the sounds, but always failed. These voices seemed only audible to him, accompanying him alone.
Although he treasured these memories of the past, they still trickled away irresistibly over time. Elvis was gradually forgetting — forgetting when he had enlisted, forgetting what his comrades looked like, and sometimes even his own name.
Elvis would always look down at his ashen, icy pale palms, knowing clearly that one day he would completely become a lost soul, but as long as Dragonsaerie still stood, he would never put down his shield.

story.text:
Clovis realized earlier than the other children the magnitude of human malice. 
The day before, he had still been the son of a respected knight, and the people smiled obsequiously before him, hoping to reap even a smidge of benefit from his father. 
The next day, he was condemned as the child of a traitor, and people spat at him on the streets. Children his age tied him up and threw him into an abandoned basement, and he was only discovered when a servant came to clean it. 
Since that day, he has known that human nature cannot be trusted.

Princess Acilia is an exception. 
She is the most noble person in the entire country, while he is the son of a lowly traitor. Clovis never imagined that they would ever cross paths. 
But that changed one day, when she stopped the children who were bullying him and brought him to the camp of the Knight Order of Platinum to treat his wounds. "We shouldn't judge people by their birth," she said, her face serious and sincere in spite of her youth. 
From then on, he has pledged his loyalty to her, and her alone.

Clovis knows that he can never become a real knight. 
He doesn't mind it, though, for he is happy to be a shadow, to be the rumored "Black Ranger". As long as he can contribute his strength to the Princess, everything will be worthwhile. 
Princess Acilia once promised him that once she became Queen, she would restore his honor and grant him a real knighthood. But to Clovis, all these don't matter. 
All he knows is that if he dies on the battlefield one day, he will still remember the girl who offered him a helping hand that day, all those years ago.

story.text:
You awoke in the Chaos Universum with no memory of your past. The Unstill had set a trap to revive the "Child of Chaos," and you, as the 1,000th sacrifice, had lost most of your soul.
You journeyed onward and defeated the Child of Chaos, but He split into several fragments that scattered across the Material Plane.
Then appeared the Dark Lady — the Dragon God, Mother of Dragons. She accused you of releasing her prisoner and threatening the world's order. Thus, you were given a mission: travel to the Material Plane and reclaim all fragments of the Child of Chaos.
Your first destination was Nytheria, now a forest wholly consumed by darkness. The Blue Oak had withered, the wood elves' faith had collapsed, and their god Nythurys had remained silent for centuries.
A boy named Lorentheel guided you to purify three wood elf altars, revive the Blue Oak, and ultimately defeat the Green Dragon to obtain the first fragment — known in the Material Plane as "Meteorite Crystals."
Just then, you heard that eerie voice again...

Your quest next brought you to the bustling and fertile plains of Lumina, home to the largest kingdom of mankind, the Dragonsaerie Empire.
After a series of coincidences, you were caught up in a great war that affected all of southern Adenthia. You became the Princess's comrade-in-arms, slaying a corrupted orc chief and ultimately destroying the root of all the disasters — the violet dragon Grumag disguised as the Grand Wizard.
In the very place where the violet dragon had perished, in his own lair, another Meteorite Crystal revealed itself to you. Behind the curtain, an order known as the Penultima also emerged, with their loyalty to the Child of Chaos.

Following the clues of the Meteorite Crystals, you reached your final destination — Teneebria in the Hypogean District.
This place had been completely corrupted by the inquietum, with the Rot running rampant. The rulers of the deep elves resorted to exile and lockdowns to contain the corruption's spread.
To reach the Corrupted Meteor Zone where the Meteorite Crystal was located, you traveled with the fugitive Ergander. After overcoming countless obstacles, you finally entered the City of Unyielding Silk. There, you discovered Queen Sacredeia of the deep elves had transformed into a Fallen Soul due to the inquietum's corruption, just like the former royal family.
When you destroyed Sivesta, the Corrupted Queen and source of the Fallen Souls, the final Meteorite Crystal appeared.
Behind the curtain, the Child of Chaos descended once more, revealing your full destiny. You and the Child of Chaos were two parts of a divided soul, two sides of the same coin. And the one who had split you apart was the instigator of it all — Tiamat, the Supreme Dragon God... your mother.

story.text:
Talwer twitched his nose as he scratched the cap on his head with his sharp, blackened claws. 
He was certain that there were several goblins active in this area, but they had all fled upon his arrival. Talwer smirked, but the poison flowing through his veins made the expression look crooked and fierce. 
They were afraid of him! Yes, it was only natural for prey to fear their predators.

Goblins are often hated and feared for their tendency to gather in groups, much like a colony of ants crawling on a sand dune. 
But Talwer is different. He is a lone wanderer, a terrifying bandit who roams the underground like a ghost. His style of hunting with poison is too vicious and ruthless, even for his own kind. 
The goblins have driven Talwer out, but that has only made this nightmare of a goblin harder to deal with.

Long, long ago — before the madness took root — Talwer was not the deranged creature he is today.
The goblin no longer recalls when he first stumbled upon that colossal toadstool, nor how its vibrant hues and intoxicating fumes ensnared him. Now it clings to his skull like a second skin — is it a hat? A grotesque new organ? Such distinctions have melted away in his poisoned mind.
The fungus pulses with his thoughts, yet its toxins only weave blissful delirium through his synapses.

story.text:
The ice-blue blade is dragged on the ground and leaves a trace.
Olgan holds it silently and patrols in the dim mist in the depths of the Vale.
This place under a cliff is unfrequented; however, this minotaur repeats his work every day. Wake up, patrol, fall asleep and then wake up again.
Nearly no one comes here. It also means that those who do come here could be trespassers.

He doesn't care about what he is protecting, neither is he interested in knowing about it.
Olgan's mind is simply preoccupied with his duty. He is loyal, rigid, and never slacks off. And he never tries to do better.
Maybe that's why Olgan was designated to guard this treasury in the first place.
Reckless souls once tried to steal the treasure here — those were the days when the minotaur's blade drank deep.

Olgan knows his master is not the owner of this treasury.
No one ever enters it, not even its current possessor. Even though his master cannot access the treasure within, he is unwilling to let it fall into anyone else's hands.
They guard this place like they guard a prison.
The minotaur doesn't care about all this. He never inquires about his master's identity and the treasure's situation.
Even so, from those thieves that never returned, he finally heard that legend: This treasury has the source of magic and the truth of this world.

story.text:
Shook bared his teeth with a threatening scowl.
"Enough, show my master some respect!" Shook swept his hands in front of the giant rat mount, causing the Three Ears members to lean in attentively.
He turned his head back to glance up at his master, Rook, mounted atop the giant rat, before turning back around.
"Must I repeat myself? Open your ears! Negotiations are all well and good, but only if they abide by my master's rules."

It was many years ago that Shook became the steward of the Three Ears boss.
He was much younger then than he is now, and Rook wasn't yet the boss of the Three Ears, but back then Rook had shown amazing potential and stood out among Zeffi's adopted children.
Perhaps seeing him as promising, the prophet brought Shook to her adopted son to clear the way for him.

Shook worships the powerful — a natural inclination in a world where strength and cunning hold sway.
Yet even servility has its limits. For this loyal retainer, one line remains inviolable: Rook's supreme authority.
From the beginning, Shook has watched his master ascend as the underworld's puppetmaster. Never has he considered it shameful to kneel — only a fool would fail to recognize Rook's brilliance.

story.text:
Using his claw hammer, Dallbam struck the solid rock formation with a wallop. Rubble flung from the rock, smacking into the surrounding gnomes at work.
"Right! That's all for today, eh?"
The squad leader ventured to Dallbam. Getting no response as the gnome carried on mining, the leader shrugged, gesturing to the others to keep their distance from him.
Taking a look at the state of him, the leader spoke, "He's lost his marbles. Leave him be, let's go."

No-one saw it coming.
Dallbam and his younger brother Gegnu were working in the crystal mine at that time. Even though they were close to the forbidden area known as the Cursed Zone, the gnomes continued digging downwards.
Of course, they struck a bounty of magic crystal.
But also, the crystal borne curse came with it.

Dallbam wasn't trapped by this supposed curse.
Crystallized body? So what? He crafted special mining lamps from this crystal, and his hardened body could protect him from all manner of harm.
His greatest love was foremost for the mines, so now mining was an even greater joy.
"A curse?" Dallbam, eyes glued to the mine, cannot face the truth, "This is clearly the crystal's blessing!"

story.text:
The rays of noon light shines on Martina's platinum shield, haloing it with a brilliant light.
As a knight of the Order of Platinum, and aide-de-camp to second in line to the throne, Princess Acilia, she holds promise in the hearts of all.
The citizens of the Dragonsaerie Empire's capital often speak of Martina and Acilia as bearing a resemblance — the same beauty, the same keenness.

Martina hefted her massive weapon, spearing her foe upon its spikes before slaming the impaled body to the earth. A final thrust drove the barbed steel home through armor and bone alike.
Though her rank excused her from such risks, the princess’s adjutant stood unwavering in every battle’s vanguard.
This was no mere pursuit of glory — it was conviction. What right had she to demand soldiers’ loyalty if she would not share their baptism of blood?

Martina never hesitates to proclaim her devotion to Acilia. She credits the Princess’s recognition as the turning point in her life.
Attaining her current position stems not merely from finding her rightful role, but also from Acilia’s unwavering commitment to her principles — a revelation that taught Martina to charge forward without regard for others’ opinions.
Through Martina’s influence, the Order of Platinum Knight has become inextricably bound to the Princess’s cause.

story.text:
Priest Dorkuraz coughed, the voices around him lowering ever so slightly.
"This winter will be tough", the frost troll's gravely voice stated to the kinsfolk around him. "The outlander humans, the foolish wood elves, the starving creatures of the Snowladen Mount — all are as hungry as we are. Don't waste your energy on futile bickering, young'uns." 
"Gramps" rapped his staff again and spoke somberly. "Now, silence, listen to me. "

Dorkuraz has yet to complete the ritual sacrifice to the mountain spirits.
The frost trolls respect those with extensive experience and ancestral revelations. They consider these "Gramps" to be the leaders of the community. Dorkuraz actually does not meet these conditions. Nevertheless, in this frigid land, creatures instinctively choose leaders who will prolong their survival.
This brooding, steely frost troll meets that criterion.

Sylvania Mountain has been silent for too long.
The frost trolls survived in this freezing snowscape by relying on Dorkuraz's ruthless wit. However, as time passed, Dorkuraz began feeling that knowledge was no longer enough to satisfy his appetite.
He was keen to forge a bond with the mountains, and to that end it didn't matter how many ill-fated travelers he filled the lake with. He was confident he would succeed one day. 
But Lake Chastity sparkles just silently as always.

story.text:
Tathlyn saw everything.
The wind's whispers across the Increscent, the trampled grass where foes had passed — too many to count.
Yet the elven archer remained motionless, his silence deeper than the forest shadows.
To act too soon was to fail. The true moment — that split-second when string must meet ear and arrow find its mark — would reveal itself only to an archer who breathed the art like wine.

The elves of the Increscent conferred upon him the moniker, Eyes of Clairvoyance.
Elves naturally boast superior distance vision, but Tathlyn's eyesight excelled beyond that of his peers.
This distinction swiftly brought him to prominence as a mentee, but hindered his career as a mentor: Something that Tathlyn found straightforward, was not so readily understood by his pupils.

Tathlyn's silence was as constant as the moon's phases.
Some elves attributed it to his bow's companionship — to that hunter's patience honed by decades of reading foes' flinches and footfalls, where sound betrayed more than it revealed.
But the keener-eyed among them recognized a deeper sight at work. Beyond his legendary archery, beyond even his hawk's vision, Tathlyn perceived the Increscent's unfolding dramas with an oracle's clarity.
Ever he found the perfect vantage. Ever his judgments rang true.

story.text:
Hegio slid his silver-keen rapier back into its scabbard, watching as the defeated soldier crumpled before him, clutching his stomach with a pained groan.
"Too hasty," he observed coolly.
Since Princess Acilia had named him the guard captain of the city, he'd become accustomed to both the barracks' endless drills and the way soldiers constantly underestimated him, first for his delicate features, then for behaviors.
He never considered himself one to glorify violence. But as the orcish shadow loomed ever darker over the realm, choices grew scarce. Of this much he was certain: his blade would follow Princess Acilia's banner until the last star fell from the sky.

Hegio is well aware of the rumors circulating in the city's streets and alleyways. 
He knows what people think of him, how they secretly see him as a freak — even refusing to share a room with him. 
"How can a pansy like him ever fight?" they mock. But this has never fazed him, for he is intelligent enough to find his place in this hedonistic land. 
Smiling, he raises his glass to toast a handsome tavern server nearby.

In his youth, Hegio once dreamt of a utopia. 
It would be a place where people lived with neither worry for their next meal or the clothes on their back, nor sin or harm. As long as there was love, then everyone belonged. However, that fantasy was quickly shattered by the harsh realities of the empire before him. 
Hegio knew better than anyone about the Church's and Wizard Guild's evil deeds, and even became involved in their conspiracies to secure the standings of the Princess and the Knight Order. 
However, deep down, he still yearns for the ascension of a new king and the arrival of a fresh era — he earnestly hopes that this won't be just a mere fantasy.

story.text:
Garian stifled a yawn behind his glove.
This aristocratic revelry was the same tiresome song for the hundredth time — the gorging, the whispered intrigues, the music loud enough to drown thought, the dancers pounding the floor like a battalion on march.
Guards keeping order weren't permitted so much as a sip of wine, and for the clan leader's most seasoned sentinels, dereliction was unthinkable. So they stood as living statues... mostly.
A single thief nabbed tonight, some fool of a servant filching trinkets. Dreadfully dull.
Another yawn threatened — then froze halfway. His eyes locked onto a small figure slipping through the shadows.
"Young mistress," Garian murmured, already steering her gently from the cacophony, "this racket will sour your humors. Let's get you to bed."

Garian never minded slacking off for a moment beneath the Stolperd's majestic white owl family crest.
He was too old now, and he had a family, so he didn't want to fool around with those young whipper snappers. He was happy not disturbing the young ones.
Staying by himself was fine. Finishing work on the dot, lounging in his rocking chair before the warmth of the hearth at home — he was content with such a life.
Too many times Garian had borne witness to the insanity wrought by the pursuit of the forbidden. He felt that uneventful days were the most in need of protection.

Garian had loved his wife fiercely. When death took her, he sealed his heart away — all but one chamber.
That remaining space belonged wholly to Felicity. Not because the girl would one day wear the clan's mantle, but for the way her laughter had filled the manor's hollow halls as she grew. Her frail frame worried him; her stubborn kindness humbled him. For her, he'd move mountains with his bare hands.
"May these old bones last long enough to stand guard when you take the throne," the usually carefree sentry often thought — perhaps the only earnest prayer left in him.

story.text:
People often believed that dwarves should keep their feet firmly planted on the ground and their eyes glued to the floor, never to dream of flying in the sky. However, there were some dwarves who had other beliefs. 
There was one dwarf who not only enjoyed looking up at the sky, but also loved storms, thunder, and lightning. He relished the sensation of rain pattering against his body, and felt roused by the power of each clap of lightning. 
One night, when a storm was approaching, his young self sneaked out of the warm safety of home and climbed to a great height, eager to immerse himself in another storm. However, he had arrived too early, and all he could see when he looked up were billowing dust gray clouds. Suddenly a lightning bolt flashed through the darkness, coincidentally striking the crown of his head.

The dwarf's fate was completely altered by this accidental lightning strike. He was bedridden for an entire three months before he barely recovered, and was forever left with snaking lightning scars all across his body. 
During his recovery, the bored dwarf suddenly discovered that his originally thick, clumsy fingers could now manipulate intricate components. 
Even before he was able to get out of bed and walk, he had already built a flying contraption. Unfortunately, he crashed heavily onto the ground during its test flight, which rendered him bedridden once again. 
However, it was thanks to this feat that he successfully joined the ranks of the aerial dwarves.

With that, Nimbus was born. Since he had not been killed by that storm, he would become the storm itself. 
He longed to lift himself off the ground and into the sky. Aerial warfare, perilous crashes, hair-raising explosions... None of these killed him, and so his flying journey continued. 
His mechanical wings were charged using the power of lightning, while his attacks rained down like storms. 
He ventured far from the ground that he was born on, flying through the skies as he protected everything he cherished above the ground and below the skies.

story.text:
Deverick dragged yet another body from a cell.
Their clothes weren't too dirty, the boots were undamaged. Someone would want them.
Silence is a virtue for corpse collectors, and Deverick had long grown accustomed to conversing with himself in his mind. He dragged the corpse through the long, squalid prison corridors, unmoved by the incessant wailing coming from behind the wrought iron doors all around him.
I hope these poor sods find solace soon. At least then their souls would be free, he thought.
These cells are never empty. When this lot dies, it fills with the next lot.
Deverick will never lack for work.

The iron cell door devoured prisoners one by one, and when it gaped open again, it mostly regurgitated corpses.
Those former scholars of the Vale, driven mad by their pursuit of forbidden power, had been dragged from their cushioned studies and thrown into this abyss. Through endless mental torment, they spent their last vestiges of vitality in frenzied howling, until finally, one day, they fell silent forever.
Then it was Deverick's turn. He would haul away these empty vessels, strip them of worldly attachments, and harvest whatever organs still held value for the researchers before decay set in.
What remained would be committed to flames, the ashes scattered into the earth as final rest. A brief eulogy would be spoken, heard by none but the dead and their keeper.

Deverick's career began quite by accident.
He had accepted a job as a bodyguard, escorting a scholar back to the Vale. Little did he know that the scholar would lose his mind overnight in the Vale. The reward hadn't been paid, so Deverick was forced to wait. After waiting for a few days, the scholar ended up dying in prison.
He had no relatives. Thinking he might recover his expenses by taking the dead scholar's effects, Deverick set about collecting the body. What awaited him, however, was a fleshy mess and a pool of gore that barely clung to the skeleton. The organs had been cut out, and the rest left to rot. Turning his head to the side, he observed a similar scene in the next cell along.
He disposed of this body, as well as the one in the next cell, then the next one, and the next...
Deverick has remained there ever since. Why? He has no idea.
Most likely because... there's no shortage of bodies in the cells.

story.text:
Upon hearing a loud crashing noise, Follie's brow furrowed reflexively. 
It seemed like Journ's experiment had, predictably, failed again. 
Though she acknowledged that her uncle's idea was rather good this time round, and that its blueprint was also brilliantly creative, it was simply... too idealistic! And too dangerous! 
Regrettably, Journ had refused to listen to her suggestions and insisted on giving it a try. Follie sighed and made her way to the laboratory they shared.

When Follie first sought refuge in Journ's laboratory, her heart had purely brimmed with enthusiasm and joy. 
A brilliant scholar naturally possesses a captivating allure to like-minded spirits, and her uncle was precisely such an individual — they even shared a common passion for magic and machinery. 
Unfortunately, not every idea can be brought to fruition, and though Journ's enthusiasm was pretty great, it could also be vexing at times. 
After witnessing a countless number of anticipated failures, Follie could no longer rein in her cynicism towards Journ — it was something she always reflected upon after the fact, but fortunately, Journ never paid any mind to it.

From the bottom of her heart, Follie harbors no loathing for her uncle's single-minded enthusiasm. 
Before she came to Teneebria, she had worked in other places before. However, most of the researchers she had met focused too much on the potential of failure and failed to perceive the minuscule, yet very real, possibilities of success in their work. 
Though it was bothersome to her when Journ frequently turned the laboratory into complete chaos, Follie would still quietly clean up his messes for him. 
Of course, her uncle would offer a helping hand as well, if he happened to spare the slightest bit of attention from his experiments.

story.text:
Gitouna set down her hammer, studying her newest creation with a critical eye. The blade gleamed cold and deadly sharp.
Beneath her heavy helm, the dwarf's eyes crinkled with unmistakable pride.
An apprentice she might be — but craftsmanship speaks louder than titles, and Gitouna's work had already set her apart from her peers.
On her finest works, she always left her mark: a delicate botanical sigil burned into the steel.

She hailed from a northern clan in the distant frost-reaches.
There, Gitouna had mastered all their traditions — only to find herself stifled by their stubborn ways. Though the clan boasted many revered smiths, their adherence to antiquity blinded them to new methods flourishing beyond the mountains.
While other forges embraced innovation, her people clung to old anvils like crutches.
Gitouna refused such stagnation. Her craft burned within her — a forge-fire that would never wane.

Gitouna isn't one to hide her competitive streak.
She has a sturdy build and her strong constitution has got her to where she is now. Incidentally, it has also had her mistaken for a male on occasion.
It is certainly the case that there are plenty of male masters among her colleagues, and she strives to sharpen her skills to one day surpass them.
If you have ambition, why pretend you don't? Especially in a world full of rivalries, a desire to disguise one's aspirations will only be frowned upon by other dwarves.

story.text:
Shink briskly puts syrup and juice into a jug and then shakes it with claws.
A wonderful aroma spreads slowly, attracting all drunkards' attention in the tavern.
"It's not suitable for you totally drunk men," says the ratfolk with a smile. She looks around and finds her target.
Shink gracefully approaches and hands over the jug, "And for you, customer, it's the perfect time for such a drink."

No one recalls when Shink first appeared at the tavern, let alone when she took over as owner.
Scanty needs its drinking holes. Truth be told, the whole bleeding world does. These are the channels where information flows, where wrath simmers, sorrow drowns, and malice finds willing ears.
But keeping such a place demands more than silver-tongued charm.
Good thing Shink's hands work as well as her mouth does. Whether behind the bar or in back alleys, she's always known how to survive.

If one salary is not enough, then earn two.
Shink never complains that she has too few coins, and she does put her heart into the running of the tavern.
Of course, her primary income comes from the Three Ears. After all, she has lived in this town for a long time as a newsmonger.
Maybe when the Three Ears needs Shink to leave, this tavern will get a new boss.

story.text:
Kailes offers a quiet prayer.
The daily regime has come to an end. Most of the Crescent Order's adherents have departed, the twilight afterglow falling on the window, casting a light upon the side of her face.
For Kailes, however, the day is not yet over. Arbiter Ardreth notified her earlier that a particular trial would require her assistance.
For the sheen, Kailes will never refuse a mission or request from the Order.

She loved everything about the Crescent Order.
Of course, it wasn't in her nature to vocalize this fanaticism. Kailes preferred to show restraint and competency before her kin.
Other subtle expressions of her fervor could be seen in the embroidered crescent moon motif on her garments, and not strictly her vestments.
It was the loveliest of motifs, and her pious devotion guided her sense of beauty.

Kailes seldom had chance to meet with the archpriestess, therefore savored it.
Mithrasea would rarely utter a word, yet Kailes couldn't help but capitalize on that sole opportunity to consult and discuss with her about the teachings of the Crescent Moon in their entirety.
But, for some inexplicable reason, the blind seer always breathed a soft sigh when they conversed.
Kailes couldn't comprehend — not yet. Perhaps, as the woman said, understanding would come when she finally stood face-to-face with her own destiny.

story.text:
The bitter cold of Iskalland demanded strong drink to drive it out.
No, no, not even a roaring hearth-fire could do the work. The deep chill of Iskalland must be conquered with liquor, for this cold seeps into your very bones, and only spirits can kindle warmth from within.
Such was Duling's unshakable doctrine of drinking. Ever did he harbor some lingering frost in his veins, and ever was he glad to help his comrades banish their own. Round after round they drank, tankards clashing like war-horns, laughter shaking the rafters. Duling's face glowed like forge-coals, his white beard trembling like a blizzard's breath.

Duling carries a reputation for generosity and boisterousness. He’s the sort who stands by his friends — anyone can trust him at their back, provided he isn’t blackout drunk. Between one tavern table and the next, combat serves as his diversion, the spoils buying ever-sweeter draughts.
Even when his furious wife and children throw him out, he just scratches his head with a shrug, inevitably seeking solace at the bottom of another glass.

Iskalland is bitterly cold.
In lucid moments, the chill seeps into Duling's bones — for he always sees them: the frozen corpses of his comrades after that fateful battle, their remains stiffening on the icy plains as howling winds pile snow upon them, layer after layer.
They remain forever young in that year. The Duling of today has decades those boys never lived to see.
Again and again, he raises his mug and whispers their names. This one's for you — he declares silently before draining it in a single gulp.
Iskalland's chill demands strong liquor.
A roaring hearth is far from enough... only the fire of spirits can melt this frozen grief.

story.text:
Thurnus impatiently pounded on the table and let out a boozy belch.
Fine! You reckon I don't know these rules and regulations, rookie? Yelled the dwarf. I've been part of the Guard far longer than you! Tend to your own affairs before you start fussing over my business!
That said, Thurnus shakily rose to his feet, propping himself up on the table to prevent him from crashing to the floor.
He'd had a little too much to drink last night and needed to hurry home for a nap.

Thurnus and his brother Gardrus both wear the fortress guard's insignia, though the elder dwarf's tenure runs deeper.
But unlike those green recruits who polish their ideals like ceremonial armor, Thurnus knows better than to worship hollow notions of honor.
Work is work — coin is coin.
The true dwarf's delight begins when the paymaster's ledger closes: a tavern bench groaning under his drunken weight, or the warm curve of a woman's hip against his calloused palm.

The growing number of young, foolish recruits in the guard displeased Thurnus.
More hands to share the work were welcome, of course, as he appreciated the extra rest time.
But too many of these greenhorns failed to show proper respect to seasoned veterans like himself, even daring to question his decisions at times. This was unacceptable, and Thurnus wasn't one to let such insolence slide.
Everyone makes mistakes, and Thurnus never missed an opportunity to teach the rookies a lesson they wouldn't forget.

story.text:
Ihuicatl released her magic slowly, letting it surge and swirl around her staff. 
Her fondness for magic was a little different from the other lizardfolk, who balked at learning minor spells with insignificant power outputs. 
However, Ihuicatl had her reasons for favoring them. 
Powerful magic had great destructive capabilities, but often ended things... too quickly. To her, the torment that makes life unbearable often stems from smaller and subtler things.

She doesn't appear to be someone who is difficult to approach. 
Ihuicatl had specially trained her voice to sound more pleasant and soothing than that of her fellows, so that she seemed more open and flattering. 
This has not only granted her many advantages, but has also helped to conceal her true, vengeful nature. 
Ihuicatl may not openly declare it, but nothing ends well for those who provoke her wrath.

Revenge has always been a beloved theme in dramas.
Ihuicatl fully appreciates its value. She detests the idea of maintaining peace at all costs, since such weakness only leads to losing what's rightfully hers.
When taking revenge, it must be executed cleanly and thoroughly, leaving no trace of involvement when the target meets their end.
The eyeball mounted on her staff serves as proof: it came from a beast that once scratched her eye. She personally gouged out its orb, and with that act, her irritation vanished completely.
